and metabolic modules from scRNA-seq. (B) Violin plots of module scores for glycolysis, mitochondrial
stress, nuclear-encoded OXPHOS, and mitochondrial-encoded OXPHOS signatures in AT2 cell scRNA-
seq dataset. (C) GSEA of lineage-traced AT2 cells from WTΔSftpc and Usp30ΔSftpc mice under homeostatic
conditions.
3. Determine if USP30 is expressed in transient cell states (DAPT/PATS/K8+) and whether
knockout in AT2 cells impacts these populations post-injury.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestions. In response, we have analyzed
Usp30 expression in transient cell states and quantified KRT8+ cells in both global and AT2-
specific Usp30 KO mice (Figures S1H, S3D, S5K and S5L in the revised manuscript).
Usp30 is universally expressed in all the cell types of mouse lungs, including in KRT8+
intermediate cells (DAPT/PATS/ADI) (Figure A). We observed a significant increase in KRT8+
cells in the alveolar regions of Usp30 KO lungs (Figure B), along with a higher percentage of
SFTPC-lineage-traced KRT8+ cells and RAGE+ AT1 cells in AT2-specific Usp30 KO lungs
(Figures C and D). These findings suggest that Usp30 KO promotes AT2 cell proliferation and
facilitates their differentiation of AT2 into mature AT1 cells, thereby enhancing alveolar
regeneration.
Figure legends: (A) Dotplot of Usp30 expression in all cell types from scRNA-seq. (B) Representative
immunofluorescence images and quantification of KRT8+ cells in lung sections from WT and Usp30-/-
mice on day 18 post-bleomycin (WT: n=9 mice; KO: n=8 mice). Scale bars: 100 μm. (C) Representative
immunofluorescence images and quantification of Sftpc-lineage-traced cells (tdTomato+) expressing
KRT8 in Usp30ΔSftpc and control mice on day 14 (n=7 mice / group). Scale bars: 100 μm. (D)
Representative immunofluorescence images and quantification of lineage-labeled cells expressing RAGE
on day 14 (n=7 mice / group). Data in B-D represent mean ± SEM. p values were analyzed by Student's
t-test.
4. Evaluate potential effects of USP30 deletion on distal bronchiolar stem/progenitor cells
(secretory cells, BASCs, LNEPs).
Response: We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestions. In response, we have
performed the following experiments to evaluate the potential role of USP30 in these cell types:
1) Secretory cells: Since there are no suitable surface markers to enrich secretory cells from
USP30 KO mice, we used Scgb1a1-CreER; R26-mTmG mice to flow sort secretory cells,
which were then cultured in 3D organoids and treated with the USP30 inhibitor MF094.
MF094 treatment did not significantly affect colony formation or cell proliferation (Figures
A–C).
2) BASCs: Bronchioalveolar Stem Cells (BASCs) are rare at the bronchioalveolar duct
junction, making it difficult to isolate and culture them. Instead, we examined BASC cell
(ZsGreen+ tdTomato+) number in the Scgb1a1-CreER; Sftpc-DreERT2; H11-ZSGT mice
on day 8 post bleomycin, which remained comparable between MF094-treated and vehicle
groups (Figure D).
3) LNEPs: LNEPs give rise to KRT5+ cells in the damaged alveoli following influenza
infection.2, 3 These cells are also rare, making it difficult to isolate and culture them. As an
alternative, we assessed KRT5+ cell expansion in WT and USP30 KO mice to indicate
LNEP activity. No differences were observed between WT and KO groups in KRT5+ cell
expansion post influenza (Figure E)
In summary, due to the limited experimental tools and systems available, we were unable to
fully evaluate the role of USP30 in the bronchiolar stem/progenitor cells. Our preliminary results
suggest that USP30 deletion or inhibition seems not significantly affect the proliferation of
secretory cells, BASCs or LNEPs. However, further studies are needed to confirm these
findings. We would be happy to include these data as a supplementary material in the
manuscript if the reviewer feels that it would enhance the manuscript.
Figure legends: (A) Schematic diagram of the experimental design for secretory cell organoid culture. (B
and C) Quantification of Colony Formation Efficiency (CFE) (Scale bars: 500 μm) (B) and EdU
incorporation (Scale bars: 20 μm) (C) in Scgb1a1-trace organoids treated with Vehicle or MF094 (n=4
droplets / group). (D) Quantification of BASCs (ZsGreen+ tdTomato+) in Scgb1a1-CreER; Sftpc-DreERT2;
H11-ZSGT mice (n=3 mice / group) on day 8 post bleomycin (Scale bars: 50 μm). White arrows indicate
BASCs. (E) Representative immunofluorescence images and quantification of KRT5+ cells in WT and
Usp30-/- lungs on day 14 post-influenza (n=12 mice / group). Scale bars: 200 μm. Data in B-E represent
mean ± SEM. p values were analyzed by Student's t-test.
5. Provide clarification on the design of the floxed allele and possible reasons for limited
recombination efficiency in AT2-specific KO mice (Figure S3B). Could this be related to the
sequence length between two loxP sites in the floxed USP30 allele, making excision less
efficient even with the robust Sftpc-CreERT2 driver?
Response: We thank the reviewer for the insightful suggestion. We have sequenced the
genome of AT2-specific KO mice and found the sequence length between two loxP sites is
1,276 bp (Figure A). According to literature, optimal recombination is achieved when loxP sites
are spaced by 1.0–4.0 kb.4, 5
We then tried to detect USP30 protein levels to determine the knockout efficiency. However,
due to the low abundance of endogenous USP30 levels, we could not detect USP30 by western
blotting. We employed Tyramide Signal Amplification (TSA) in immunofluorescence staining to
amplify the signals. USP30 has been reported to primarily localize to mitochondria and
peroxisomes.6 TSA staining showed mostly cytoplasm signals along with cell surface signals.
Quantification of the cytoplasm signals confirmed ~50% decrease of protein levels in lineage-
traced AT2 cells (Figure B).
Figure legends: (A) Genomic sequencing analysis validating the 1,276 bp distance between loxP sites in
AT2-specific KO mice. (B) Representative immunofluorescence images and quantification of USP30
levels specifically within uninjured Sftpc-traced AT2 cells (tdTomato+) (n = 8 fields pooled from 3 mice
/ group). Scale bars: 10 μm. Data in B represent mean ± SEM. p values were analyzed by Student's
t-test.
6. Include lineage-tracing data (tdTomato) in AT2-specific KO experiments (Figure3) to better
distinguish AT2-derived regeneration from bronchiolar stem cell contributions. More precise
quantification of AT2 proliferation (tdT+ vs tdT–) is needed.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the suggestions. We have now quantified EdU
incorporation in tdT- AT2 cells. While Usp30-KO tdT+ AT2 cells exhibited significantly higher
proliferation rates compared to WT tdT+ AT2s (Fig. 3M), tdT- AT2 cells in Usp30ΔSftpc mice
showed comparable proliferation rates compared with that in WT mice (Figure A). To evaluate
the relative contribution of surviving AT2 and bronchiolar stem/progenitor populations in the
proliferating AT2 cells post influenza infection, we analyzed the lineage composition of the
proliferating AT2 pool. tdT+ AT2 cells constituted >80% of total EdU+ AT2 cells in both WT and
Usp30 cKO mice (Figure B). We would be happy to include these data as a supplementary
material in the manuscript if the reviewer feels that it would enhance the manuscript.
Figure legends: (A) Quantification of EdU incorporation specifically within tdT- AT2 population in Sftpc-
CreERT2 mice (PBS: n=3 mice / group; influenza: n=13 mice / group). (B) Stacked bar graph showing the
proportion of lineage-labeled (tdT+) and non-labeled (tdT-) cells within the total EdU-positive AT2
population. Data represent mean ± SEM. p values were analyzed by two-way ANOVA (A).
Minor Points:
1. The statement that USP30 KO “does not affect” fibroblasts or macrophages may be too
strong according to limited data here; consider rephrasing.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion and we have revised the text accordingly
in Line 252–260 and Line 437.

Wu et al. investigate the role of USP30-mediated mitophagy in promoting alveolar regeneration
following lung injury. The authors used genetic and pharmacological approaches targeting
Usp30 to demonstrate that loss of USP30 enhances mitophagy and restores mitochondrial
function in AT2 cells, thereby protecting them from apoptosis and promoting regenerative
capacity. The findings are interesting and provide a fresh insight into the cellular mechanisms
of tissue repairing. The study nicely shows that Usp30 deletion reduces AT2 apoptosis and
promotes proliferation across multiple lung injury models. It can be further strengthened to
examine the link between USP30 loss and changes in the AT2 cell transcriptomic profile
with or without injury, providing evidence how USP30 loss enhances AT2 stem cell
activity at the molecular level. A few other minor issues are listed below.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable suggestions. To understand the molecular
mechanism underlying enhanced stem cell activity, we have performed bulk RNA-seq on
lineage-traced AT2 cells isolated from Usp30ΔSftpc mice and controls, both at baseline and on
day 14 post bleomycin and influenza injury. These data have been incorporated into the revised
manuscript as Figures S6 and S8.
At baseline, Usp30-deficient AT2 cells showed enrichment of proton motive force-driven
mitochondrial ATP synthesis, mitochondrial translation and respirasome assembly (Figures A
and B), in support of improved mitochondria function. Pathway analysis in Usp30-KO AT2 cells
at baseline showed enrichment of Notch, Wnt, MAPK, and PI3K-AKT signaling, which are
important for stem cell activity and cell proliferation (Figure C).
Following bleomycin injury, Usp30-KO AT2 cells downregulated immune responses and

attenuated lymphocyte activation and recruitment observed in GSEA (Figures G-I). Pathway
analysis showed enrichment of PI3K-AKT and MAPK signaling.
These findings suggest Usp30 KO in AT2 cells improved mitochondrial function and
upregulated multiple signaling pathways, leading to enhanced stem cell activity.

1. The significance of the studies, especially the translational potential, will be enhanced with
evidence of higher expression of USP30 in AT2 cells of human lung fibrotic diseases like IPF.
Similarly, if changes in ubiquitination and protein levels of VDAC1 observed in the current
mouse studies are relevant for the human fibrotic disease.
Response: We appreciate the reviewers’ valuable suggestions. In response, we have
performed western blot of USP30 and VDAC1 in human IPF and healthy donor lungs. Our
results showed significantly elevated protein levels of USP30 and its substrate, VDAC1, in IPF
lungs compared to healthy donors (Figure A). Due to the lack of suitable antibodies for human
USP30 and VDAC1 for immunofluorescence staining, we analyzed a publicly available scRNA-
seq dataset of IPF lungs (GSE136831)12 to examine USP30 and VDAC1 expression. USP30
mRNA levels were upregulated in multiple cell types, including AT2 cells, in IPF lungs, whereas
VDAC1 mRNA levels were not increased in AT2 cells from IPF lungs (Fig. B and C), This
suggest that the regulation of VDAC1 by USP30 occurs at the post-translational level rather
than through transcriptional regulation. The western blot results have been incorporated into
the revised manuscript as Fig. 2G. We would be happy to include the transcriptome data as a
supplementary material in the manuscript if the reviewer feels that it would enhance the
manuscript.
Figure legends: (A) Representative immunoblots and quantification of USP30, VDAC1, and fibrotic
markers (ACTA2, COL1A1) in whole lung lysates from healthy donors (Normal: n=4) and IPF patients
(n=6). β-Actin served as the loading control. (B and C) Dot plots visualizing USP30 (B) and VDAC1 (C)
mRNA expression across distinct epithelial cell subsets derived from the GSE136831 dataset. Data in A
represent mean ± SEM. p values were analyzed by Student's t-test.
2. scRNAseq data do not align with the other set of data of the manuscript. For example, the
proportion of myofibroblasts that the authors show increase by IFA are not shown, nor the
cluster of fibrotic fibroblasts CTHRC1+ that produce high levels of ECM. These changes will
confirm the effect in fibrosis by the absence of USP30. Similarly, it would be important to define
the cluster of proliferating AT2 to confirm the EdU and organoid experiments. Additionally, there
is lack of AT1 cell cluster. The AT2-AT1 cluster shown in the UMAP data has a limited
proportion in comparison with the abundant Ager+ staining shown in Figure 2.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising these points. In response, we have analyzed the
scRNA-seq data to validate our experimental findings.
1) Fibroblasts: we analyzed lung fibroblast subpopulations in the scRNA-seq dataset.
Pathologic fibroblast marker Cthrc1 was enriched in the "Proliferating fibroblast" cluster,
while myofibroblast marker Acta2 was enriched in both "Peribronchial fibroblast" and
"Proliferating fibroblast" clusters (Figure A). Usp30 KO mice exhibited a marked reduction
in the proportion of "Proliferating fibroblast" and "Peribronchial fibroblast" clusters
compared to WT (Figure B). Usp30 deletion did not significantly affect gene expression
related to apoptosis, proliferation, or differentiation in any individual fibroblast
subpopulation (Figure C), which is consistent with our in vitro functional assays. These
findings are included in the revised manuscript as Fig. S1J, S1K and S4I.
Figure legends: (A) Dot plot displaying expression of fibroblast markers across each distinct subcluster.
(B) Proportion of fibroblast subpopulations identified by scRNA-seq in bleomycin-injured lungs. (C) Violin
plots of module scores for gene signatures across fibroblast subtypes.
2) AT2 Proliferation: We analyzed AT2 cells in the scRNA-seq dataset and found the
proportion of Mki67+ AT2 cells was decreased in Usp30-KO AT2 cells compared to WT
controls (Figures D and E). This discrepancy likely reflects different timepoints of the
experiments. The scRNA-seq was performed on day 18 post injury, which is fibrotic phase
in bleomycin model, while EdU assay was performed on day 8 when endogenous AT2
cells are highly proliferating (epithelial repair phase). While Usp30-KO AT2 cells exhibited
higher proliferation rates during repair phase, the lower proportion of proliferating AT2 cells
in KO mice on day 18 suggests a faster return to homeostatic quiescence.
Figure legends: (D) Feature plots showing the expression of the proliferation marker Mki67 in AT2 cells
from WT and Usp30 KO lungs on day 18 post-bleomycin injury. (E) Quantification of the percentage of
Mki67+ cells within AT2 cell population.
3) Lack of AT1 Cells: AT1 cells are thin, large and fragile, which make them particularly
susceptible to the tissue dissociation methods required for single-cell suspensions.13
However, immunofluorescence staining was effective in capturing these cells. In our
scRNA-seq, we did not identify a distinct population solely expressing the mature AT1
markers. Instead, we observed a population expressing both AT1 marker Ager and the
intermediate marker Krt8, which we defined as “AT2-to-AT1 cells” (Figure F).
Figure legends: (F) UMAP plot of epithelial cell subpopulations (left) and feature plots showing the
expression of AT2 (Sftpc), transition (Krt8), and AT1 (Ager, Hopx, Aqp5, Pdpn) markers (right) in
bleomycin-injured lungs on day 18.
3. Interestingly, studies in Figure 2 and 2S show that AT2 cells of WT mice in naïve conditions
have active apoptosis in contrast to AT2 from USP30 KO. Authors suggest that this apoptosis
is related to high levels of VDAC protein. It is unclear what is the stimuli for overexpression of
VDAC1 in naïve healthy AT2 cells to mediate apoptosis. Furthermore, transcriptomic data is
needed to demonstrate that changes in VDAC in USP30 deficient AT2 cells are not associated
with transcriptional changes and only are related to changes in ubiquitination and protein
degradation.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the helpful suggestions. In Fig. 2C, we measured the
apoptosis of primary AT2 cells isolated from WT and Usp30-KO mice and treated with or without
bleomycin in culture. In naïve conditions, apoptosis levels reflect the inherent stress of culturing
primary cells, with less than 3% cells undergoing apoptosis. In contrast, bleomycin treatment
induced ~15% cells undergoing apoptosis. Usp30 KO significantly inhibited apoptosis both
under baseline and post bleomycin injury.
VDAC1 is a key player of mitochondrial-dependent apoptosis by forming channels on the outer
mitochondrial membrane, facilitating the release of cytochrome c into the cytosol.14, 15
Overexpression of VDAC1 in HEK293 T cells resulted in less than 0.5% apoptotic cells under
baseline conditions, whereas approximately 3% of cells underwent apoptosis following
bleomycin injury (Fig. S3C in the revised manuscript). We think the observed apoptosis in naïve
conditions is primarily due to the stress associated with 2D culture.
To investigate the regulation of VDAC1 by USP30, we performed transcriptional analysis. No
significant differences were observed in Vdac1 mRNA levels between WT and KO cells under
baseline conditions, either in the bulk cell RNA-seq of FACS-sorted primary AT2 cells (Figure
A) or primary AT2 cells in 2D culture (Figure B). These results together with the western blots
in bleomycin and IPF lungs (Fig. 2F and 2G in the revised manuscript) suggest that the
regulation of VDAC1 by USP30 occurs at the post-translational level. We would be happy to
include these data as a supplementary material if the reviewer feels that it would enhance the
manuscript.
Figure legends: (A) Vdac1 TPM values from bulk RNA-seq of FACS-sorted AT2 cells (n=3 biological
replicates / group). (B) qRT-PCR analysis of Vdac1 and Usp30 in primary AT2 cells cultured in 2D
monolayers (n=5 biological replicates / group). Data represent mean ± SEM. p values were analyzed by
Student's t-test.
4. The high levels of mtROS in AT2 from USP30 KO mouse are in contrast to the increase in
maximal respiration shown in the seahorse studies for KO cells. High maximal OCR generally
is associated with a state of low mtROS generation and mitochondrial fitness. Furthermore, it
is unclear why there are not changes in the mitochondrial TMRM and mitochondrial mass
between mouse strains if mitophagy is induced differently between groups. Simultaneous
analysis of these two parameters might help to give a better understanding as well as
complementary markers of autophagy like p62 protein levels, and ubiquitination of Parkin to
analyze mitophagy. Furthermore, studies of mitophagy flux in the AT2 cells might be also useful.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s constructive suggestions. Since OCR was measured
in cultured primary AT2 cells, we have further examined the dynamic changes of ROS levels,
mitochondrial TMRM, mitochondrial mass and mitophagy flux in these cells. These data have
been incorporated into the revised manuscript as Figures S3E-S3I.
1) ROS levels: Usp30-KO cells exhibited moderately elevated baseline mtROS and cytosolic
ROS levels, along with a transient increase of mtROS following bleomycin injury, which
then decreased (Figures A and B). In contrast, WT cells showed an accumulation of
cytosolic ROS after injury. These findings suggest Usp30-KO cells effectively mitigate
injury-induced oxidative stress.
2) TMRM and Mitochondrial Mass: No significant differences in TMRM and mitochondria
mass were observed between WT and Usp30-KO AT2 cells at baseline (Figures C and D).
However, following injury, mitochondria mass gradually increased until 6 hours and then
declined at 8 hours in WT cells, while KO cells exhibited an accelerated decline starting at
4 hours, suggesting enhanced mitophagy. Consistent with this, KO cells had increased
TMRM at 6 hours post injury.
3) Mitophagy Flux: Based on the dynamic changes observed in Figures A-D, we performed
western blotting for p62 and LC3B to examine the mitophagy flux at 4 hours post injury.
Bafilomycin A1 (BafA1) inhibits lysosomal acidification, resulting in a blockage in
autophagic flux and accumulation of autophagosomes. In the absence of BafA1, Usp30 KO
cells exhibited lower levels of p62 and higher levels of LC3B-II compared to WT cells
(Figure E), suggesting enhanced mitophagy. In the presence of BafA1, Usp30 KO cells
accumulated significantly higher levels of LC3B-II and p62, indicating a higher rate of
autophagosome formation and fusion with lysosomes.
In summary, Usp30-KO cells exhibited enhanced mitophagy, increased mitochondrial
biosynthesis and elevated ATP synthesis. After injury, they displayed a transient increase in
mtROS followed by a decline. This phenomenon is consistent with the concept of mitohormesis,
where mild mitochondrial stress, such as a brief increase in mtROS, induces beneficial adaptive
responses that enhance cellular function and cause a long-term reduction of oxidative stress.16-
bleomycin (2 mg/mL) for 0h–8h. Panels show mt-ROShigh population (A), cROS MFI (B), mitotracker MFI
(C), TMRMhigh population (D) (n=8 biological replicates / group). (E) Representative immunoblots of
autophagic flux markers (LC3B, p62) in primary AT2 cells. Cells were treated with bleomycin (2 mg/mL)
for 4 hours, with or without Bafilomycin A1 (BafA1, 100 nM) for the final 2 hours. β-Actin served as the
loading control. Data in A-D represent mean ± SEM. p values were analyzed by two-way ANOVA (A-D).
5. Figure 1M do not show markers of cell type to define if AT2 cells have been analyzed for the
colocalization of mitochondria and LC3B. it seems that USP30 deficiency increase levels of
LC3B.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the suggestion. In response, we have included AT2
specific marker SFTPC in the immunofluorescence staining by optimizing a four-color
immunofluorescence protocol (Mito-Dendra2, SFTPC-Cy5, LC3B-Cy7 and DAPI). These data
have been incorporated into the revised manuscript as Figures S2C and S2D.
1) AT2-Specific Mitophagy Analysis: We quantified the mitophagy index (ratio of LC3B+
mitochondrial area to total mitochondrial area) specifically within SFTPC+ AT2 cells.
Usp30-KO AT2 cells exhibited a significantly higher mitophagy index compared to WT
controls under both homeostatic and injury conditions (Figures A and B).
2) LC3B Signal Intensity: We quantified LC3B intensity in AT2 cells and confirmed that
signal intensity was elevated in the Usp30 KO group (Figure C). This increase reflects
enhanced recruitment of the autophagy machinery driven by the stabilization of ubiquitin
chains on damaged mitochondria, suggesting enhanced autophagic flux rather than a
blockage. As further validated by LC3B western blotting (Figure S3I in the revised
manuscript), lysosomal inhibition induced a significant additional accumulation of LC3B-II
in KO cells.
Figure legends: (A and B) Representative multicolor immunofluorescence images (A) (Scale bars: 5μm)
and quantification (B) of mitophagy index in lung sections from Usp30 KO and WT mice expressing the
mito-Dendra2 reporter (n ≥ 70 representative fields pooled from 3 mice / group). Sections were co-stained
for SFTPC (Cy5) and LC3B (Cy7). Mitophagy index was calculated as the ratio of LC3B+ mitochondrial
area to the total mitochondrial area specifically within SFTPC+ AT2 cells. (C) Quantification of the mean
fluorescence intensity (MFI) of LC3B signal specifically within the SFTPC+ AT2 cell population. Data
represent mean ± SEM. p values were analyzed by two-way ANOVA.
6. The authors in line 162 suggest enhanced mitochondrial biosynthesis in AT2 from USP30
KO suggested by mitochondrial morphology and number. Complementary studies of markers
of mitochondrial biogenesis and dynamics are recommended to support the statement.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestion. In response, we have examined
gene expression related with mitochondrial biogenesis and dynamics using scRNA-seq data.
Usp30-KO AT2 cells displayed increased expression of Ppargc1a, the master regulator of
mitochondrial biogenesis, and replication/transcription machinery (Polrmt, Twnk) as well as
higher expression of mitochondrial genes that encode essential components of the
mitochondrial respiratory chain (Figure A). GSEA analysis confirmed that enrichment of
mitochondrial translation, respirasome assembly and proton motive force-driven mitochondrial
ATP synthesis in Usp30-KO AT2 cells (Figure B). Usp30-KO AT2 cells also exhibited
downregulation of fission genes (Fis1, Dnm1l) and fusion markers (Mfn2, Opa1), with the
exception of Mfn1, which was upregulated. These data have been incorporated into the revised
manuscript as Figures S2E.
Figure legends: (A) Dot plot of representative genes corresponding to mitochondrial biogenesis, dynamics
and metabolic modules from scRNA-seq. (B) GSEA of lineage-traced AT2 cells from WTΔSftpc and
Usp30ΔSftpc mice under homeostatic conditions.
7. Figure 4B shows inhibition rate of the Compound MF094, however it will be more specific to
show the effect of the compound on the ubiquitination of a known mitochondrial protein target
of USP30.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the helpful suggestion. In response, we have examined
the ubiquitination of phospho-Ser65-Ubiquitin (p-S65-Ub), which serves as a robust proxy for
the ubiquitination status of mitochondrial USP30 substrates.19 MF094 treatment resulted in a
dose-dependent accumulation of p-S65-Ub in mouse AT2 cell line (MLE12 cells) treated with
mitochondrial uncoupler Carbonyl cyanide m-chlorophenyl hydrazone (CCCP). This finding
confirms that MF094 effectively inhibits USP30 deubiquitinase activity by preserving ubiquitin
chains on mitochondria, thereby enhancing the p-S65-Ub signal (Fig. S9 in the revised
manuscript).
Figure legends: Representative immunoblots of Phospho-Ser65-Ubiquitin in MLE12 cells treated with
various concentrations of MF094 and CCCP (10 μM). Tom20 and β-Actin served as loading controls.
Minor concerns
1. The measurements for OH-Pro for bleomycin and influenza pneumonia lung models have
more data points than other experimental variables, suggesting than more than 1 sample per
lung mouse was analyzed. There is not a description in this respect on methods. Please clarify.
Response: We apologize for causing confusion. Each data point represents an independent
biological replicate, corresponding to a distinct mouse in the animal study. For the OH-Pro
measurements shown in Fig. 1J and S5F, we pooled mice from 2 independent experiments, as
the OH-Pro window in bleomycin model typically shows less than a 2-fold difference.
2. The USP30 protein expression and levels after deletion were not analyzed
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion. We tried to detect USP30 protein levels
in the mouse lungs. However, due to the low abundance of endogenous USP30 levels, we
could not detect USP30 by western blotting. We employed Tyramide Signal Amplification (TSA)
in immunofluorescence staining to amplify the signals. USP30 has been reported to primarily
localize to mitochondria and peroxisomes.6 TSA staining showed mostly cytoplasm signals
along with cell surface signals. Quantification of the cytoplasm signals confirmed significant
protein deletion in Usp30-/- lungs (Figure A) and specifically within lineage-traced AT2 cells in
cKO mice (Figure B). These data have been incorporated into the revised manuscript as
Figures S1E and S5C.
Figure legends: (A) Representative immunofluorescence images (left) and quantification (right) of USP30
signal intensity in lung sections from uninjured WT and Usp30 KO mice (n = 10 fields pooled from 3 mice
/ group). Scale bars: 10μm (B) Representative immunofluorescence images (left) and quantification (right)
of USP30 levels specifically within uninjured Sftpc-traced AT2 cells (tdTomato+) (n = 8 fields pooled from
3 mice / group). Scale bars: 10μm Data represent mean ± SEM. p values were analyzed by Student's t-
test.
Reference

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: Authors have adequately addressed my questions and concerns.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: The authors have addressed this reviewer's concerns.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The authors have addressed several of the previously raised concerns. One point that would benefit from further clarification is the persistence of Krt8⁺ interstitial epithelial cells in USP30 KO mice following injury. While the authors interpret this finding as evidence of improved alveolar regeneration, alternative explanations should also be considered.
Here the assessment was performed at day 18 post-injury, a time point at which transitional AT2–AT1 cells are typically expected to decline as repair progresses. For instance, Strunz et al. 2020 (Nature Communications)reported that Krt8⁺ transitional cells appear early after bleomycin injury, peak around day 9, and gradually decrease, becoming nearly undetectable by day 21. In addition, persistent Krt8⁺ transitional cells have been linked to dysfunctional or maladaptive repair responses, including associated to mitochondrial abnormalities and activation of the ISR, as described by Han et al. Nature 2023.
Therefore, it would be helpful for the authors to discuss whether the sustained presence of Krt8⁺ cells might also reflect stalled or arrest differentiation of AT2 cells, rather than unequivocally improved regeneration. Additional analyses across multiple time points, as well as more detailed quantitative and qualitative characterization (e.g., via single-cell RNA sequencing), would strengthen the interpretation. Clarifying whether Krt8⁺ cells are detectable in naïve USP30 KO mice would also provide valuable context. Addressing and/or discussing these points would enhance the robustness of the conclusions regarding alveolar regeneration in the USP30 KO model.

Response to the reviewers' comments:
We sincerely thank the reviewers and the editors for their constructive suggestions and positive feedback, which have significantly strengthened our manuscript. In the revised manuscript, we have updated the discussion as requested by the reviewer and addressed all formatting, policy, and compliance requests outlined in the editorial checklist.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
Authors have adequately addressed my questions and concerns.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the positive feedback and constructive suggestions,
which have significantly strengthened our manuscript.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have addressed this reviewer's concerns.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s positive feedback and insightful suggestions, which
have significantly improved our manuscript.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have addressed several of the previously raised concerns. One point that would
benefit from further clarification is the persistence of Krt8⁺ interstitial epithelial cells in USP30
KO mice following injury. While the authors interpret this finding as evidence of improved
alveolar regeneration, alternative explanations should also be considered. Here the
assessment was performed at day 18 post-injury, a time point at which transitional AT2–AT1
cells are typically expected to decline as repair progresses. For instance, Strunz et al. 2020
(Nature Communications) reported that Krt8⁺ transitional cells appear early after bleomycin
injury, peak around day 9, and gradually decrease, becoming nearly undetectable by day 21.
In addition, persistent Krt8⁺ transitional cells have been linked to dysfunctional or maladaptive
repair responses, including associated to mitochondrial abnormalities and activation of the ISR,
as described by Han et al. Nature 2023.
Therefore, it would be helpful for the authors to discuss whether the sustained presence of
Krt8⁺ cells might also reflect stalled or arrest differentiation of AT2 cells, rather than
unequivocally improved regeneration. Additional analyses across multiple time points, as well
as more detailed quantitative and qualitative characterization (e.g., via single-cell RNA
sequencing), would strengthen the interpretation. Clarifying whether Krt8⁺ cells are detectable
in naïve USP30 KO mice would also provide valuable context. Addressing and/or discussing
these points would enhance the robustness of the conclusions regarding alveolar regeneration
in the USP30 KO model.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the constructive suggestions. We agree that the
persistence of KRT8+ transitional cells, such as those induced by ISR activation, represents
dysfunctional or maladaptive repair, as elegantly described by Han et al. (2023)1. To directly
address whether KRT8+ cells in the USP30 KO mice reflect stalled differentiation or improved
regeneration, we have analyzed the KRT8+ cells using both immunofluorescence staining and
RNA-seq analysis at baseline and post injury. Our data support improved regeneration,
demonstrated by increased AT2 cell proliferation and differentiation. Notably, both KRT8+ cells
and AT1 cells increased, indicating that the cells were not stalled in a transitional state. These
findings have been incorporated into the revised manuscript as Fig. S9, with relevant discussion
added in Lines 429-439.
1. Krt8+ transitional cells do not spontaneously emerge in naïve USP30 KO mice.
As requested by the reviewer, we assessed KRT8+ transitional cells in naïve mice.
Immunofluorescence staining of lung sections showed an absence of KRT8-expressing cells in
the alveolar regions of saline-treated WT and USP30 KO mice (Figure A). At baseline, KRT8
expression was confined to the airway epithelium, which served as an internal positive control
for our staining. These data show that USP30 deletion alone does not spontaneously induce a
transitional state.
Transcriptomic analysis of flow-sorted Sftpc-lineage traced cells from saline-treated mice
showed the expression of transitional markers (Krt8, Cldn4, and Cdkn1a) was comparable
between WT and Usp30ΔSftpc mice (Figure B), further confirming that no spontaneous induction
of KRT8+ cells occurred in USP30 KO.
2. Transcriptomic profiling suggest rapid resolution of the transitional state post injury.
Transcriptomic analysis of Sftpc-lineage traced cells from bleomycin-injured lungs on day 14
showed that transitional markers (Krt8, Cldn4, and Cdkn1a) were highly upregulated in the WT
mice, indicating induction of transitional cells. However, this induction was significantly lower in
the USP30 cKO mice (Figure B), suggesting AT2 cells were not stalled in the transitional state
in the absence of USP30. Immunofluorescence staining in Figs. 2H-2R and S3D demonstrated
USP30 KO mice showed a significant increase in the proliferation rate of AT2 cells, as well as
an expansion of AT2 and AT1 cell-covered areas and an increase in KRT8+ cell numbers.
These results suggest that enhanced AT2 cell proliferation leads to a larger pool of AT2 cells,
contributing to the increased numbers of KRT8+ and AT1 cells observed in USP30 KO.
Consistent with these findings, AT2-specific USP30 KO mice also exhibited higher proliferation
rates of AT2 cells and increased differentiation towards KRT8+ and AT1 cells. Together, these
data suggest USP30 deletion significantly enhances AT2 cell proliferation and differentiation,
leading to improved regeneration.
Figure legends: (A) Representative immunofluorescence images of KRT8 (white) and DAPI
(blue) in the lungs of saline-treated WT and Usp30 KO mice. Scale bars: 100μm. Similar
immunofluorescence staining patterns were consistently observed in at least three biologically
independent animals per group. (B) Bulk RNA-seq analysis of Sftpc-lineage AT2 cells sorted
from WTΔSftpc and Usp30ΔSftpc mice at baseline (Saline) and 14 days post-bleomycin injury. Bar
plots show the expression levels (Transcripts Per Million, TPM) of established AT2-to-AT1
transitional and senescence markers, including Krt8, Cldn4, and Cdkn1a.
References
1. Han, S. et al. Mitochondrial integrated stress response controls lung epithelial cell fate. Nature
620, 890–897 (2023).

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Alveolar Type II cells (AT2s) are the stem cells responsible for both lung alveolar homeostasis and
regeneration. Mitochondrial dysfunction in AT2 cells has been implicated in both chronic and acute
injury-induced alveolar diseases, including idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and viral pneumonia.
However, the role of mitochondrial homeostasis in post-injury lung repair and regeneration remains
elusive. Here we demonstrate that genetic depletion of Ubiquitin Specific Peptidase 30 (USP30), a
negative regulator of mitophagy, boosts mitophagy and restores mitochondrial function in AT2 cells,
leading to protection from injury-induced apoptosis and enhanced stem cell activity. Both global and
AT2-specific Usp30 knockout (KO) promote alveolar regeneration, protecting the mice from bleomycin-
induced lung fibrosis and influenza pneumonia. Moreover, pharmacological inhibition of USP30
effectively alleviates these conditions. Together, our findings reveal a previously underappreciated role
for mitophagy in lung injury and repair and highlight USP30 inhibition as a promising therapeutic
strategy for treating alveolar diseases.

---

## Introduction

Mitochondria are vital energy factories and key regulators of cellular communication, lipid metabolism,
calcium homeostasis, and apoptosis.1-10 Mitochondrial dysfunction, characterized by reduced ATP
synthesis and the accumulation of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS), has been
implicated in numerous human diseases, including neurodegenerative diseases and respiratory
conditions like IPF and viral pneumonia.11-17 Mitophagy, the process by which damaged mitochondria
are removed and recycled, coordinates with mitochondrial dynamics and biogenesis to maintain
mitochondrial function.18, 19 Impaired mitophagy results in the accumulation of damaged mitochondria
and contributes to the pathogenesis of various diseases.

Accumulating evidence suggest that mitochondrial dysfunction and abnormalities in mitophagy
contribute to respiratory diseases. For example, IPF is a chronic and devastating lung disease caused
by repeated injuries to the alveolar epithelium, leading to abnormal or failed alveolar repair.20-25 AT2
cells, which act as stem cells in the alveoli, from patients with IPF exhibit an accumulation of damaged
mitochondria, impaired mitophagy and reduced expression of PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1).26, 27
PINK1, along with Parkin, plays a crucial role in mitochondrial quality control. Pink1-/- mice show
enlarged mitochondria, defective mitochondrial function and increased susceptibility to lung fibrosis.26
Parkin deletion also exacerbates lung fibrosis in mouse model.28 The absence of mitochondrial fusion
proteins mitofusin1 (MFN1) and mitofusin2 (MFN2) in mouse AT2 cells leads to spontaneous lung
fibrosis.29 On the other hand, viral pneumonia is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide,
which may lead to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).30, 31 The severity of the infection is
often associated with mitochondrial dysfunction. For example, oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS)
impairment, modeled by Ndufs4 deficiency, can exacerbate influenza pathogenesis by reprograming
lung epithelial metabolism to enhance viral attachment.32 Ripk2 knockout impairs mitophagy,
enhances NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and increases mortality upon influenza virus infection.33
These findings underscore the link between these respiratory diseases and mitochondrial dysfunction
and support that restoring mitochondrial homeostasis may confer therapeutic benefits on patients.

USP30 is a universally expressed deubiquitinase that is primarily localized to the outer mitochondrial
membrane and antagonizes Parkin-mediated ubiquitination, thus functions as a key negative regulator
of mitophagy.34, 35 It preferentially removes ubiquitin chains connected via Lys6 and Lys11 linkages.35-
37 Knockout or inhibition of USP30 rescues the defective mitophagy in parkin or pink1 mutant flies,
functionally protects dopaminergic neurons in Parkinson’s disease mouse model and reduces
oxidative stress in human neurons,34, 38, 39 validating USP30 as potential therapeutic target for
Parkinson’s disease. Recently, the knockout of Usp30 has also been shown to improve heart failure
in mice caused by cardiomyocyte-specific knockout of carnitine palmitoyl transferase 2 (CPT2) by
promoting mitophagy.40 However, it is unknown whether USP30 plays a role in lung diseases.

Here, we demonstrated mitochondrial dysfunction in both IPF lungs and influenza induced pneumonia.
Using both genetic and therapeutic models, we showed that either USP30 knockout or inhibition
protects the mice from bleomycin induced lung fibrosis and influenza induced pneumonia.
Mechanistically, USP30 depletion reduces the apoptosis of AT2 cells after injury and increases AT2
cell proliferation capacity, thus restricting alveolar injury and promoting alveolar regeneration,
respectively. These data therefore support USP30 as a promising therapeutic target to treat injury
induced pulmonary diseases such as IPF and influenza pneumonia by promoting lung repair and
regeneration.

## Results

Usp30 KO mice are protected from bleomycin induced lung fibrosis
A re-analysis of published transcriptomic data of pulmonary fibrosis (PF) lungs41 (GSE110147)
revealed “oxidative phosphorylation”, “aerobic respiration”, “ATP synthesis coupled electron transport”
were the top Gene Ontology (GO) terms enriched in the downregulated genes (Fig.1A, S1A),
suggesting defective mitochondrial function in PF lungs. Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA)
elucidated significant downregulation of oxidative phosphorylation and mitophagy in PF lungs (Fig. 1B
and 1C). In align with the analysis, the expression levels of PINSK1 and PRKN were negatively
correlated with fibrillar collagen expression (Fig. S1B). Re-analyzing published single-cell RNA
sequencing (scRNA-seq) data of IPF lungs42 (GSE135893) further revealed a significant
downregulation of oxidative phosphorylation in the mesenchymal, epithelial, and immune cells (Fig.
S1C and S1D). Mitophagy was significantly decreased in the epithelial cells, endothelial and immune
cells of IPF lungs, with the most pronounced changes occurring in epithelial cells (Fig. 1D). These
results collectively demonstrated that in the patients with IPF, mitochondrial dysfunction is associated
with impaired mitophagy, which correlates with the degree of fibrosis. Given mitochondrial dysfunction
has been reported to contribute to fibrogenesis,26-29 we hypothesized that enhancing mitophagy may
restore mitochondrial function and thereby inhibit lung fibrosis.

To test our hypothesis, we generated a Usp30, a gene encoding a negative regulator of PINK1 and
PARKIN-mediated mitophagy pathway,34 knockout (KO) mouse model by deleting exon 4 of the Usp30
gene. The knockout efficiency was confirmed by qRT-PCR (Fig. 1E). We further validated protein
depletion using immunofluorescence with Tyramide Signal Amplification, which confirmed reduction
of USP30 protein levels in the lung tissue (Fig. S1E). Usp30-/- mice developed and bred normally
without gross histological phenotypes, consistent with previously reported.38, 43 Bleomycin model is a
widely used lung fibrosis model. Upon bleomycin challenge, Usp30-/- mice exhibited significantly less
body weight loss compared to wild-type (WT) control mice (Fig. 1F and 1G). Masson’s trichrome
staining revealed a substantial reduction in the fibrotic areas in Usp30-/- mice (Fig. 1H and 1I). Usp30
KO significantly reduced hydroxyproline levels and fibrotic gene expression (Fig. 1J and 1K).
Immunostaining of the myofibroblast marker ACTA2 confirmed a significant decrease in myofibroblast
accumulation (Fig. 1L). These data collectively support that Usp30 KO alleviates bleomycin induced
lung fibrosis.

To examine whether Usp30 KO enhances mitophagy, we crossed Usp30 KO mice with PhAMexcised
mice, which exhibit ubiquitous expression of mito-Dendra2 fluorescence localized specifically to
mitochondria.44 By quantifying the proportion of mitochondria colocalizing with LC3B+ autophagic
puncta, we were able to quantify the mitophagy levels in mouse lungs. Our results demonstrated
Usp30 KO increased the level of mitophagy under both homeostatic conditions and following
bleomycin injury (Fig. 1M).

Usp30 deletion improves mitochondrial function and promotes alveolar regeneration
To explore the potential mechanisms by which Usp30 KO alleviates pulmonary fibrosis, we performed
scRNA-seq of the bleomycin injured lungs on day 18 post injury, analyzing both CD45+ immune cells
and CD45− non-immune cells (Fig. S1F). After rigorous quality control, we retained a total of 78,379
high-quality cells and identified 21 distinct cell types based on established marker genes (Fig. S1G
and S1H).42, 45-48 Usp30 was universally expressed in all the cell types (Fig. S1H). Changes in cell
composition between WT and Usp30 KO groups were then compared. Consistent with decreased
severity of fibrosis, Usp30 KO lungs exhibited a reduced proportion of "Proliferating" and
"Peribronchial" fibroblast clusters, which were highly enriched for the pathological fibroblast marker
Cthrc1, Postn and the myofibroblast marker Acta2 (Fig. S1I-S1K). The most pronounced change was
observed in AT2 cells, which were significantly more abundant in the KO group compared to WT group
(Fig. S1I).

AT2 cells serve as alveolar stem cells, capable of self-renewal and differentiation into mature alveolar
type 1 (AT1) cells, which are essential for gas exchange.49-51 AT2 cells are also responsible for
maintaining alveolar surface tension.52 Given the critical role of AT2 cells in maintaining alveolar
integrity and their reliance on mitochondria for energy production and survival, 49, 53 we next assessed
mitochondrial morphology, mitochondrial function and apoptosis of USP30-deficient AT2 cells.
Previous studies have reported frequent enlarged and swollen mitochondria in AT2 cells from both
IPF patients and Pink1-/- mice as shown by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images.26 To
assess mitochondrial architecture, we employed scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and 3D
reconstruction. Under baseline conditions, the mitochondria of Usp30-KO AT2 cells displayed smaller,
more condensed cross-sectional areas compared to WT controls (Fig. S2A and S2B). Following
bleomycin injury, mitochondria in WT AT2 cells exhibited marked swelling and a globular morphology,
while Usp30-KO AT2 cells showed significantly reduced mitochondrial size and a fragmented, short
rod-like morphology. Quantitative analysis revealed that while injury induced a significant increase in
mitochondrial counts, there was no significant difference in the number of mitochondrial per cell
between WT and KO groups (Fig. S2A). Therefore, we hypothesized that Usp30 KO may enhance
mitophagy and mitochondrial biosynthesis in AT2 cells.

Next, we examined mitophagy, mitochondrial biogenesis and dynamics in the AT2 cells. The AT2
marker SFTPC was co-stained with LC3B in PhAMexcised mice, with or without Usp30 deletion. Usp30-
KO AT2 cells exhibited significantly higher levels of mitophagy compared to WT controls both under
both homeostatic conditions and following bleomycin injury (Fig. S2C), along with elevated LC3B
signal intensity (Fig. S2D). These data suggest that USP30 deletion enhances mitophagy levels in
AT2 cells.

We also examined gene expression related with mitochondrial biogenesis and dynamics using scRNA-
seq data. Usp30-KO AT2 cells displayed increased expression of Ppargc1a, the master regulator of
mitochondrial biogenesis, as well as higher expression of mitochondrial genes that encode essential
components of the mitochondrial respiratory chain (Fig. S2E). Furthermore, Usp30-KO AT2 cells
maintained higher mitochondrial OXPHOS levels while exhibiting lower glycolysis levels and reduced
mitochondrial stress (Fig. S2F), indicating a healthier metabolic profile.

To validate the transcriptome analysis, we then assessed mitochondrial function by measuring oxygen
consumption rate (OCR) in cultured WT and Usp30-/- AT2 cells. Usp30 KO significantly increased the
maximum respiration rate, basal respiration rate, and ATP production capacity under both baseline
and bleomycin-treated conditions (Fig. 2A and 2B), suggesting improved mitochondrial function. A
higher maximum respiration rate often correlates with enhanced energy production capability, thereby
improving cell viability and function.54, 55 Bleomycin induces DNA damage, thus leading to apoptosis
of the damaged epithelial cells. 56, 57 Usp30 deletion significantly inhibited bleomycin induced apoptosis
in both AT2 cultures and bleomycin injured lungs (Fig. 2C-2F). This result was further supported by
the observation of more remaining epithelial cells in the bleomycin-injured Usp30-/- lungs on day 8,
when inflammation and injury peaked (Fig. S3A).

Next, we explored the mechanism by which Usp30 deletion inhibits apoptosis. Among the numerous
deubiquitination substrates of USP30, voltage-dependent anion channel 1 (VDAC1) has been reported
as a key player of mitochondrial-dependent apoptosis.34, 58 VDAC1 forms channels on the outer
mitochondrial membrane through oligomerization, regulating the release of cytochrome c to the cytosol,
and thereby leading to mitochondrial-dependent apoptosis.59, 60 We found VDAC1 overexpression was
sufficient to increase bleomycin-induced apoptosis (Fig. S3B and S3C). In bleomycin injured lungs,
Usp30 KO decreased VDAC1 protein levels, leading to reduced apoptosis (Fig. 2F). To validate the
clinical relevance of the USP30-VDAC1 axis identified in the mouse model, we analyzed lung tissue
samples from IPF patients and healthy donors. Immunoblotting of whole lung lysates revealed
significantly elevated levels of USP30 and its substrate, VDAC1, in IPF lungs compared to healthy
controls (Fig. 2G), suggesting a conserved regulatory role of USP30 on VDAC1 protein levels in both
mouse and human lung fibrosis and also suggesting a therapeutic potential of targeting USP30 for IPF
treatment.

Epithelial injury induces apoptosis of the damaged epithelial cells, while the surviving AT2 cells
proliferate and differentiate into AT1 cells to repair the damaged regions.61-64 We then asked if AT2
stem cell activity is impacted by USP30 deletion by using organoid cultures. Interestingly, Usp30-/- AT2
organoids exhibited significantly higher colony formation efficiency (CFE) and increased proliferation
and differentiation, resulting in a significantly greater number of proliferating AT2 cells and
differentiated AT1 cells (Fig. 2H-2N). Consistent with organoid culture results, Usp30-/- mice displayed
a significantly higher rate of AT2 proliferation following bleomycin injury (Fig. 2O and 2P), which leads
to larger areas of AT2 and AT1 cells as well as a significant increase of KRT8+ intermediate cells
(DAPT/PATS/ADI),65-68 suggesting improved alveolar regeneration (Fig. 2Q, 2R, and S3D).

To further explore the molecular basis underlying increased AT2 proliferation, we assessed
mitochondrial ROS levels, mitochondrial quantity, and changes in mitochondrial membrane potential
both in vitro and in vivo. In cultured WT and Usp30-KO AT2 cells, Usp30 KO cells exhibited moderately
elevated baseline mitochondrial ROS (mtROS) and cytosolic ROS (cROS) levels, along with a
transient increase of mtROS following bleomycin injury, which then decreased, suggesting effective
mitigation of injury-induced oxidative stress (Fig. S3E-H). There were no significant differences in
mitochondria mass and mitochondrial membrane potential between WT and Usp30-KO AT2 cells at
baseline. However, following injury, mitochondria mass gradually increased until 6 hours and then
declined at 8 hours in WT cells, while KO cells exhibited an accelerated decline starting at 4 hours,
suggesting enhanced mitophagy. Consistent with this, KO cells had increased mitochondrial
membrane potential at 6 hours post injury and enhanced mitophagy flux as evidenced by P62 and
LC3-II protein level changes (Fig. S3I).

In bleomycin-injured lungs, Usp30 KO did not affect cROS levels, mitochondrial quantity nor
mitochondrial membrane potential (Fig. S3J-S3N). Instead, Usp30 KO increased mtROS levels in AT2
cells on day 8, coinciding with the increase of AT2 proliferation on day 8, followed by a rapid decline
of mtROS on day 14 during the later stage of repair (Fig. S3K). mtROS are considered as byproducts
of efficient oxidative phosphorylation,69 but it has been reported that moderate levels of ROS can
promote basal cell proliferation.70 To test if ROS levels affect AT2 cell proliferation, we introduced
hydrogen peroxide into AT2 organoid cultures to induce ROS accumulation (Fig. S3O). Lower
concentrations of hydrogen peroxide promoted AT2 cell proliferation, while higher concentration
inhibited it (Fig. S3P and S3Q). These results suggest that Usp30 KO induced a transient increase of
mtROS in AT2 cells, thereby facilitating the repair of the epithelial barrier.

In addition to AT2 cells, we explored the potential effects of Usp30 KO on other cell types, such as
macrophages and fibroblasts. Our results showed that Usp30 KO did not significantly affect
macrophage polarization (Fig. S4A and S4B). Next, to determine if the reduction in fibrosis was due
to direct effects on mesenchymal cells, we isolated primary lung fibroblasts from Usp30 KO and WT
mice. These cells exhibited comparable proliferation rates, activation, myofibroblast differentiation,
and apoptosis levels in vitro (Fig. S4C-S4H). We also examined transcriptional profiles of fibroblasts
in vivo using the scRNA-seq dataset. Usp30 deletion did not significantly affect gene expression
related to apoptosis, proliferation, or differentiation in any fibroblast subpopulation (Fig. S4I). These
data collectively suggest that the reduced fibrotic burden in Usp30 KO mice is not due to cell-
autonomous effects on fibroblasts.

In summary, our study demonstrated that Usp30 KO significantly improved mitochondrial function,
inhibited AT2 apoptosis possibly by decreasing VDAC1, and promoted AT2 stem cell activity likely by
increasing mitochondrial ROS levels, leading to alveolar regeneration and thus ameliorated lung
fibrosis.

AT2-specific Usp30 deletion effectively mitigates bleomycin injury and ameliorates pulmonary
fibrosis
Next, we asked whether AT2-specific Usp30 KO is sufficient to induce the protective effect on
pulmonary fibrosis. To explore this, we established an AT2-specific Usp30 KO mouse model,
SftpcCreERT2;R26tdT;Usp30flox/flox (hereafter Usp30ΔSftpc). Four doses of tamoxifen injections decreased
50% of USP30 expression in AT2 cells (Fig. 3A and 3B). Immunofluorescence further validated ~50%
deletion of protein specifically in lineage-labeled AT2 cells (Fig. 3C).

Subsequently, the mice were challenged with bleomycin. Compared to control group,
SftpcCreERT2;R26tdT;Usp30wt/wt (hereafter WTΔSftpc), Usp30ΔSftpc mice exhibited significantly less body
weight loss (Fig. 3D) and less severe lung fibrosis as evidenced by Masson’s trichrome staining,
quantification of fibrotic areas, hydroxyproline levels, fibrotic gene expression and ACTA2
immunofluorescence staining (Figure 3E-3H). The apoptosis levels in Usp30ΔSftpc mice were
significantly lower than those observed in the control group (Fig. 3I), while there were more
proliferating AT2 cells and a higher percentage of Sftpc-lineage-traced KRT8+ intermediate cells and
RAGE+ AT1 cells in Usp30ΔSftpc mice (Fig. 3J-3L), indicating less alveolar injury and better alveolar
regeneration, respectively. These results demonstrated AT2-specific Usp30 KO attenuates lung
fibrosis at a similar extent as global Usp30 KO. Taken together, these results established that AT2-
specific Usp30 KO is sufficient to mitigate lung fibrosis by inhibiting AT2 apoptosis and promoting AT2
proliferation.

To unravel the molecular mechanism underlying enhanced regenerative capacity, we performed
transcriptomic profiling of primary AT2 cells isolated from Sftpc-CreERT2 mice both at baseline and
post bleomycin injury. GSEA and cumulative distribution function (CDF) analysis of AT2 cells at
baseline revealed enrichment of proton motive force-driven mitochondrial ATP synthesis,
mitochondrial translation, respirasome assembly and increased mitochondrial gene expression in
Usp30-KO AT2 cells (Fig. S5A and S5B), resembling the scRNA-seq and OCR results. Pathway
analysis in Usp30-KO AT2 cells at baseline showed enrichment of Notch, Wnt, MAPK, and PI3K-AKT
signaling, which are important for stem cell activity and cell proliferation (Fig. S5C). Following
bleomycin injury, Usp30-KO AT2 cells downregulated immune responses and senescence markers
(Cdkn1a, Cdkn2a, Cdkn2b) while upregulating AT2 identity markers (Sftpc, Etv5) (Fig. S5D and S5E).
Notably, multiple genes associated with Wnt/β-catenin signaling, FGF signaling, and Hippo-YAP
signaling, which are critical for AT2 cell regeneration after injury,71-74 were upregulated, including Axin2,
Fzd1/2, Ctnnb1, Fgfr2, and Yap1. Pathway analysis showed enrichment of PI3K-AKT and MAPK
signaling (Fig. S5F). These findings suggest Usp30 KO in AT2 cells improved mitochondrial function
and upregulated signaling pathways related with stem cell activity.

Usp30 deletion confers protection against influenza pneumonia
Given Usp30 KO protects AT2 cells from apoptosis and promotes AT2 cell proliferation, we reasoned
that Usp30 deletion may also provide beneficial effects in respiratory viral infections. H1N1 influenza
A virus (IAV) induces severe respiratory epithelial damage that may lead to acute respiratory distress
syndrome and potentially progressing to lung failure.75, 76 To monitor the dynamic changes of
mitochondria specifically in AT2 cells after IAV infection, we collected the mouse lungs on multiple
time points post infection and examined mitochondrial morphology and gene expression (Fig. 4A).
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images demonstrated that the mitochondria in AT2 cells,
identified by the presence of their characteristic lamellar bodies (LBs), from IAV infected mouse lungs
were enlarged and swollen as early as day 2 post infection, and the number of mitochondria enclosed
by autophagic vesicles increased by day 11, indicative of undergoing mitophagy (Fig. 4B). The RNA-
seq analysis of flow-sorted AT2 cells showed that mitochondrial gene expression was suppressed at
various time points post infection (Fig. 4C), suggesting defective mitochondrial function.

The role of USP30 in IAV-induced lung injury was first investigated using Usp30-/- mice (Fig. S6A). All
Usp30-/- mice survived the influenza challenge, while half of the WT mice succumbed (Fig. S6B).
Moreover, the lung function of Usp30-/- mice, as measured by arterial oxygen saturation, declined less
and recovered more quickly (Fig. S6C). Inflammatory cell counts and protein levels in the
bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) were comparable at early time points, however, significantly lower in
the KO mice by day 14, when the tissue injury peaked (Fig. S6D and S6E), suggesting the initial injury
was at similar levels, but there was less immune infiltration and tissue damage in the KO mice over
time. Consistently, cell apoptosis levels were significantly lower in the KO mice by day 14 compared
to the WT mice (Fig. S6F), suggesting Usp30 KO protects cells from apoptosis.

AT2 marker gene expression and alveolar epithelium covered areas were significantly higher in the
Usp30-/- mice (Fig. S6G-S6I). EdU labeling revealed a significantly higher proportion of proliferating
AT2 cells in the KO mice (Fig. S6J). We confirmed higher levels of mitophagy in the Usp30-/- mice after
influenza infection (Fig. S6K). Consistent with the results in bleomycin model, no significant changes
in total ROS levels (Fig. S6L and S6M), mitochondrial quantity (Fig. S6N) or mitochondrial membrane
potential (Fig. S6O) were observed. However, the levels of mitochondrial ROS exhibited more
pronounced dynamic changes in the KO group (Fig. S6P). Specifically, Usp30-/- mice exhibited higher
mitochondrial ROS levels on day 14, followed by a decline during the later phase of repair on day 24,
indicating a greater adaptability of the mitochondria.

Given the critical role of mitochondria in antiviral responses77, we examined whether Usp30 deletion
impacts virus control. No significant differences in viral load were observed between the WT and KO
mouse lungs (Fig. S6Q and S6R). Additionally, viral infection in AT2 organoids did not reveal any
notable differences in viral load (Fig. S6S and S6T). These findings indicate Usp30 deletion protects
the mice from influenza infection by decreasing cell apoptosis and promoting AT2 proliferation, but not
antiviral responses.

We then further validated the role of USP30 in IAV model using AT2-specific Usp30 KO mice.
Usp30ΔSftpc mice exhibited faster recovery of body weight and lung function than control group
following infection (Fig. 4D-4F). There were significantly less inflammatory cell counts and protein
levels in the BAL as well as cell apoptosis levels in the cKO mice on day 14 compared with that in
control mice (Fig. 4G-4I), indicating less tissue damage. Furthermore, AT1 and AT2 cell covered areas,
which represent epithelial barrier integrity, were restored at a higher extent in the Usp30ΔSftpc mice
compared to the control group (Fig. 4J and 4K). Sftpc mRNA levels were also higher in the Usp30ΔSftpc
group (Fig. 4L). Usp30-null AT2 cells showed a significantly higher proliferation rate (Fig. 4M). Taken
together, our results showed that Usp30 deletion has a conserved protective role across different lung
injury models by limiting AT2 cell apoptosis and promoting AT2 cell proliferation.

To investigate the molecular basis, we performed transcriptomic analysis on flow-sorted AT2 cells on
day 14 post infection. Usp30-KO AT2 cells exhibited a marked upregulation of cell cycle and mitotic
pathways, along with a downregulation of immune response-related genes, such as chemokines and
alarmins (Cxcl2, Ccl3, S100a8, Il1b), consistent with the attenuated lymphocyte activation and
recruitment observed in GSEA (Fig. S7A and S7B). Pathway analysis also highlighted enrichment in
PI3K-AKT and MAPK singaling (Fig. S7C). These transcriptomic findings validated the enhanced
proliferation of AT2 cells and improved tissue regeneration observed.

Pharmacological inhibition of USP30 ameliorates lung fibrosis and influenza pneumonia
Our results of global and conditional knockout mouse models demonstrated USP30 is a potential
therapeutic target to alleviate both chronic and acute lung injury. We thus tested this notion by using
MF094, a commercially available USP30 inhibitor that has been validated with highly selective
inhibitory effect both in vitro and in vivo.78-80 We first confirmed the inhibitory effects of MF094 on
USP30 enzyme activity and its impact on bleomycin-induced AT2 cell apoptosis (Fig. 5A). The results
showed that MF094 inhibited USP30 enzyme activity with an IC50 of 69.60 nM (Fig. 5B) and exhibited
a dose-dependent effect in suppressing bleomycin-induced apoptosis in mouse lung epithelial cell line
MLE12 (Fig. 5C). We also examined the ubiquitination of a known USP30 substrate, phospho-Ser65-
Ubiquitin (p-S65-Ub), which is phosphorylated at Ser65 by PINK1.81 MF094 treatment resulted in a
dose-dependent accumulation of p-S65-Ub following mitochondrial depolarization in MLE12 cells (Fig.
S8A), confirming effective inhibition of USP30 deubiquitinase activity.

We then tested the effects of MF094 in vivo. MF094 was intraperitoneally injected daily starting on the
third day after bleomycin injury until tissue harvest on day 14 (Fig. 5D). Mice treated with the USP30
inhibitor exhibited decreased lung fibrosis severity and less myofibroblast accumulation (Fig. 5E-5I).
The apoptotic levels were significantly lower in the inhibitor treated group (Fig. 5J).

In IAV model, MF094 was daily administrated starting from the third day post-infection till day 14 (Fig.
5K). The inhibitor treated mice exhibited less body weight loss, faster recovery of body weight and
better lung function (Fig. 5L and 5M). Inflammatory cell counts and protein levels in BAL were
significantly lower in the inhibitor group (Fig. 5N and 5O). Sftpc expression as well as AT2 and AT1
covered areas were significantly higher in the inhibitor treated group (Fig. 5P-5R), while tissue
apoptosis was significantly lower (Fig. 5S). Taken together, our studies using the two lung injury
models support USP30 as a promising therapeutic target for lung injury-induced fibrosis and viral
pneumonia.
