## Methods

Ethical compliance
This research complies with all relevant ethical regulations regarding animal research and human
tissue usage. All animal studies were approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of ShanghaiTech
University (protocol: 20210928001) and were performed in compliance with ethical guidelines and the
approved protocols. The human study protocol for the use of human lung tissues was approved by the
Human Ethics Committee of Shanghai Pulmonary Hospital (protocol: K21-282), and written informed
consent was obtained from all participants prior to inclusion.

Mice
Usp30-/- mice, generated by utilizing Cas9 technology to knock out a 64 bp sequence in exon 4 (gRNA1:
5'-GGCGTCCAAGACCTCGTCCT-3', gRNA2: 5'-ATGGCAGATCTCGTCCTTTG-3'), resulting in
premature termination of the encoded protein, and Usp30fl/fl mice, created by inserting flox sites at
both ends of exon 2 via Cas9 technology, allowing for deletion of exon 2 upon Cre expression, were
purchased from GemPharmatech. Sftpc-CreERT2 mice102 were generously provided by Dr. Chuwen
Lin at Sun Yat-sen University. Rosa26-tdTomato mice103 were generously provided by Dr. Harold A.
Chapman at University of California, San Francisco. PhAMexcised mice44 were generously provided by
Dr. Yifeng Zhang at ShanghaiTech University and crossed with Usp30-/- mice to examine mitophagy
levels. All experiments were carried out using mice aged 12-20 weeks, with age and sex matched,
and mice of both sexes were used in equal proportions. The mice used in this study were housed in
the Animal Core Facility at ShanghaiTech University under pathogen-free conditions, maintained at
an ambient temperature of 20-24°C and 40-60% humidity, in a 12 hours light/dark cycle room with
water and food ad libitum. All mice used in this study were on a C57BL/6 background.

Bleomycin model of lung fibrosis
After anesthetizing the mice with isoflurane, 50 µL of bleomycin (1.6 mg/kg body weight, Nippon
Kayaku) dissolved in saline was administered into the lungs via intratracheal intubation. Both control
and experimental groups consisted of sex and weight-matched mice to minimize experimental
variation. Following the model induction, mouse body weight was monitored regularly, and the mouse
lungs were collected on days 14-18.

Influenza infection
The mice were anesthetized using isoflurane to agonal breathing and intranasally administrated with
40 µL of H1N1 influenza virus PR8 (diluted in cold phosphate-buffered saline (PBS)). The viral dose
administered was approximately 36 PFU. The H1N1 influenza virus was received as a generous gift
from Dr. Haikun Wang at the Shanghai Institute of Immunology and Infection, Chinese Academy of
Sciences. Mice were weighed three times per week and euthanized at the indicated time points for
tissue harvest.

Tamoxifen treatment
Tamoxifen (Sigma-Aldrich, T5648) was dissolved in corn oil at a concentration of 40 mg/mL. To knock
out Usp30, Usp30ΔSftpc mice and the control WTΔSftpc mice were given tamoxifen at a dose of 200
mg/kg via intraperitoneal injection every other day for a total of four injections. After a 4-week waiting
period, knockout efficiency was validated, followed by experimental modeling.

Arterial blood oxygen saturation measurement
Arterial blood oxygen saturation was assessed using the MOUSEOX Pulse Oximeter system (STARR
Life Sciences). Before measurements, the thigh of the mice were shaved. During measurement, the
mice were anesthetized with isoflurane, and readings of oxygen saturation were taken using the thigh
sensor mode. After obtaining the first successful reading, measurements were conducted for at least
2 minutes per mouse, and the stable, continuous readings were averaged as the final result for each
mouse.

Lung cell isolation
The mouse lung cells were isolated based on an established protocol.104 After perfusion and lavage,
the lungs were inflated with 1 mL of pre-cold sterile Dispase II (Gibco, 17105041, 15U/mL, dissolved
in HBSS and filtered through a 0.22 µm filter) via a catheter into the trachea, followed by 0.2 mL of
warm 1% low melt agarose (BBI, A600015, dissolved in sterile ddH2O). Individual lobes were
separated, with large airways filled with agarose discarded, and the lobes were submerged with 1 mL
of Dispase II in 50 mL tubes, rocked at room temperature for 45 minutes. The tissue was chopped
using a 10 mL pipette until no visible clumps remain. Then 10 mL of DMEM (Invitrogen, 31053036)
with 2% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Ausbian, VS500T), 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Thermo, 15140122)
and 50 U/mL DNase I (Roche, 10104159001) was added to the digested lobes, and pipetting was
performed vigorously. The mixture was swirled at 37°C for 15 minutes on a rotating platform, and the
cell suspension was filtered sequentially through 100 µm, 70 µm, and 40 µm strainers. The filtered
suspension was centrifuged for 3 minutes at 300 × g to pellet the cells. If necessary, red blood cells
were lysed by 1 mL of RBC lysis buffer (Beyotime, C3702) at room temperature for 1 minute, followed
by stopping the reaction with 5 mL of DMEM supplemented with 2% FBS and 1%
penicillin/streptomycin.

Flow cytometry
After lung tissue dissociation, cells were resuspended in DMEM supplemented with 2% FBS and 1%
penicillin/streptomycin at a density of 20 million/mL. For identifying lineage+ cells, cells were stained
with Fixable Viability Dye eFluorTM 780 (1:2000, Thermo Fisher Scientific, 65-0865-14)，FITC-
conjugated rat anti-mouse CD45 (1:1000, BD, 553080), BV711-conjugated rat anti-mouse CD31
(1:500; Biolegend, 102449), BV421-conjugated rat anti-mouse EpCAM (1:500; Biolegend, 118225),
Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated rat anti-mouse Integrin β4 (1:300; Biolegend, 123608). All cell sorting was
performed on BD FACSAria Fusion Cell Sorter. EpCAM+ cells were sorted as epithelial cells, EpCAM+
Integrin β4- cells as AT2 cells, CD45+ cells as immune cells, CD31+ cells as endothelial cells, and
EpCAM- CD31- CD45- as fibroblasts.

To assess mitochondrial-related markers in epithelial cells, BUV395-conjugated rat anti-mouse CD45
(1:300; BD, 564279), BV711-conjugated rat anti-mouse CD31 (1:500, Biolegend, 102449), BV421-
conjugated rat anti-mouse EpCAM (1:500; Biolegend, 118225), Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated rat anti-
mouse Integrin β4 (1:300; Biolegend, 123608) were used as lineage markers. Mitotracker green (200
nM; Invitrogen, M7514) was used to measure mitochondrial content, TMRM (100 nM; Invitrogen, T668)
for mitochondrial membrane potential, H2DCFDA (10 μM; MCE, HY-D0940) for cellular ROS levels,
and MitoSOX red mitochondrial superoxide indicator (5 μM; Yeasen, 40778ES50) for mitochondrial
ROS levels. Flow cytometry analysis was performed using the BD LSRFortessa X-20 and BD
FACSDiva software (version 8.0.3). Data analysis was performed using FlowJo software (version
10.4).

Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL)
After exposing the trachea of the mouse, a 20G catheter was inserted into the trachea for lavage. One
milliliter of cold PBS was instilled into the lungs, followed by gentle aspiration, repeated three times.
All bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was collected and centrifuged at 700 x g. The supernatant was
collected to measure total protein content using the BCA assay (Thermo, 23227). The cell pellet was
lysed in red blood cell lysis buffer for one minute, the reaction was stopped with PBS, and the cells
were counted using a hemocytometer.

Hydroxyproline assay
For hydroxyproline detection, the manufacturer's protocol for the hydroxyproline kit (Sigma-Aldrich,
MAK008-1KT) was followed. Mouse lung tissues were snap frozen in liquid nitrogen and ground into
a fine powder. The powdered tissue was then hydrolyzed with 1 mL of 6 M hydrochloric acid at 120°C
for 3 hours. After cooling, the hydrolysate was neutralized with sodium hydroxide. Subsequently, 5 µL
of the hydrolysate was transferred to the center of a well in a 96-well plate. The assay reagent,
containing a chromogenic agent specific for hydroxyproline, was added to each well to facilitate a color
change. Absorbance was measured at 550 nm using a spectrophotometer, and hydroxyproline
concentrations were calculated based on a standard curve generated from known hydroxyproline
concentrations.

EdU incorporation and analysis
To detect AT2 cell proliferation after bleomycin-induced injury, 100 µg of EdU (ThermoFisher Scientific,
A10044) was administered to mice via intraperitoneal injection on day 2, 4, and 6 after injury, with lung
tissue collected on day 8. The Click-iT EdU Alexa Fluor 647 flow cytometry assay kit (ThermoFisher
Scientific, C10424) were used to examine proliferating cells via FACS. For influenza-induced injury,
proliferating AT2 cells were labeled using the same method on day 8, 10, and 12 after infection, with
lung tissue collected on day 14 for analysis.

Caspase-3/7 activity assay
After grinding the snap-frozen mouse lung tissue into a powder, protein was extracted using RIPA
buffer (50mM Tris-HCl PH7.5, 150mM NaCl, 1% deoxycholate, 0.1% SDS, 1% Triton X-100)
supplemented with Protease Inhibitor Cocktail (Roche, 11697498001), 1mM phenylmethyl sulfonyl
fluoride (PMSF) and Phosphatase Inhibitor Cocktail (Sigma Aldrich, 524625-1SET). Protein
concentration was quantified using BCA assay (Thermo, 23227). An equal amount of protein was used
to detect caspase-3/7 activity with the Caspase-Glo® 3/7 Assay (Promega, G8091). Briefly, 5 µg of
total protein was diluted in PBS to a volume of 40 µL, then mixed with 40 µL of the reaction solution in
a clear-bottom 96-well plate. The mixture was shaken at 300-500 rpm for 5 minutes and incubated at
room temperature for 30 minutes. The solution was then transferred to a white opaque 96-well plate
and measured using a Spark Multimode Microplate Reader (Tecan, Switzerland). Two replicates were
set up for each sample, with the average of the two replicates as the final reading.

Masson’s trichrome staining
Trichrome stain was performed on the frozen lung sections according to the standard procedure of
Masson Stain Kit (Yeasen, 60532ES74) with modifications. Briefly, OCT embedded frozen sections
were equilibrated to room temperature and rehydrated in distilled water for 1 minute before
sequentially stained with hematoxylin for 1 minute, acidic fuchsin for 2 minutes, phosphomolybdic acid
for 5 minutes, and aniline blue for 3 minutes, with three washes with washing solution between each
staining step. After the final dehydration step in anhydrous ethanol, the sections were mounted for
microscopic analysis.

For quantitative assessment of fibrosis, stained sections were analyzed using Fiji/ImageJ software.
The color deconvolution plugin was first applied using the Masson Trichrome vector set to isolate the
collagen-specific blue channel. The threshold function was then used to select and quantify collagen-
positive areas, while total lung area was determined using the WEKA Trainable Segmentation plugin
for 2D image analysis. The percentage of fibrotic areas was calculated as the percentage of collagen-
positive areas relative to total lung areas.

AT2 organoid culture
Mouse AT2 cells were flow sorted from WT or Usp30-/- mouse lungs, resuspended at 3,000 cells per
40 μL droplet in a 1:1 mixture of AT2 Maintenance Medium (AMM)105 (without CHIR99021 and IL-1β)
and Matrigel® (Corning, 356231), plated in 24-well plates, and allowed to solidify at 37°C for 30 min
before adding 500 μL pre-warmed AMM (without CHIR99021 and IL-1β). Medium was changed every
three days. Samples were collected after 10 days of culture. For oxidative stress experiments,
organoids were treated with H2O2 (Sinopharm, 10011208) at various concentrations of 1 μM, 5 μM, or
10 μM in fresh AMM (without CHIR99021 and IL-1β) throughout the entire duration of the experiment.

To analyze the colony formation efficiency, each droplet was imaged using a Nikon TI-E microscope
in bright-field mode. Z-stack images were combined, and the number of organoids was counted using
ImageJ. In ImageJ, the image contrast was enhanced using the "Subtract Background" function. A
threshold was applied to distinguish colonies from the background. If colonies appeared clumped, the
watershed function was used to separate them. Finally, colonies were counted using the "Analyze
Particles" function, with appropriate size settings to exclude noise and adjustments to the circularity
parameter. Only organoids with more than five nuclei were included.

Influenza infection of AT2 organoids
For viral infection, AT2 organoids were initially cultured at a density of 5,000 cells in the complete AMM
medium for 10 days. Then, the droplets were digested with Dispase II (15 U/mL ; Gibco, 17105041)
at 37°C for 30-40 minutes to be released from Matrigel. One to two droplets from each group were
further digested with TrypLETM (ThermoFisher Scientific, 12604013) for 5-10 minutes to obtain single
cells for cell count reference. The rest of organoids were centrifuged, washed with PBS and then
mechanically sheared using 1 mL pipette tips to expose the apical surface for viral infection. The virus
was added at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 0.01 and incubated at 37°C for 1 hour. After infection,
the organoids were washed three times with PBS, reseeded in 40 µL of a 1:1 Matrigel:Medium mixture
in a 24-well plate at a density of 100,000 cells per well. Organoids were collected at various time points,
washed three times with PBS followed by snap frozen in liquid nitrogen for RNA extraction to measure
the viral load.

Oxygen consumption rate (OCR) measurement
Cells from AT2 organoids after 10-d culture were digested using Dispase II and TrypLETM as above
mentioned and seeded for OCTR measurement. Prior to cell plating, each well of the Seahorse XF96
plate (Aligent) was coated with Matrigel at 1:20 dilution in PBS and incubated for 2 hours at 37°C. AT2
cells were then seeded at a density of 30,000 cells per well in the complete AMM medium and allowed
to attach for 24 hours in a humidified incubator at 37°C with 5% CO₂. Eight hours prior to OCR
measurement, cells were treated with 1 mg/mL bleomycin (Vokai Biotechnology, 9041-93-4) or vehicle
control.

The Seahorse assay was performed according to the manufacturer’s protocol. The culture medium
was replaced with Seahorse XF assay medium supplemented with appropriate substrates. Plates
were equilibrated at 37°C without CO₂ for 1 hour before OCR measurements. The OCR was measured
under basal conditions and after the sequential addition of inhibitors (1.5 μM oligomycin, 1 μM FCCP,
and 0.5 μM each of rotenone/antimycin A) to assess mitochondrial function. Each measurement
included three baseline readings followed by injections of oligomycin and FCCP to evaluate ATP
production and maximal respiratory capacity, respectively. Data were analyzed using Seahorse Wave
software, and OCR was expressed in pmol/min.

In vitro mitochondrial function and mitophagy flux assay
Cells from AT2 organoids were dissociated as described above and seeded in 12-well plates pre-
coated with Matrigel (1:20 diluted) at a density of 250,000 cells per well. After 24 hours, cells were
treated with bleomycin (2 mg/mL; Vokai Biotechnology, 9041-93-4) or vehicle control. For flow
cytometric analysis, cells were digested with 0.25% trypsin at indicated time points. Mitochondrial
parameters were assessed using Mitotracker green (200 nM; Invitrogen, M7514), TMRM (100 nM;
Invitrogen, T668), H2DCFDA (10 μM; MCE, HY-D0940), and MitoSOX red (5 μM; Yeasen,
40778ES50). Data acquisition was performed on a BD LSRFortessa X-20. For mitophagy flux analysis,
cells were treated with bleomycin (2 mg/mL) or vehicle for 4 hours. Bafilomycin A1 (100 nM) was
added 2 hours prior to harvest, followed by protein extraction and Western blot analysis.

Cell line culture
MLE12 cells (ATCC, CRL-2110) were cultured in HITES medium (Dulbecco's:Ham's F12, 50:50 mix
supplemented with 2% FBS (Ausbian, VS500T), 0.005 mg/mL insulin (Tocris, 3435/10), 0.01 mg/mL
transferrin (Roche, 10652202001), 30 nM sodium selenite (Sigma-Aldrich, S9133), 10 nM
hydrocortisone (MCE, HY-N0583), 10 nM β-estradiol (Sigma-Aldrich, E2758), and 2 mM L-glutamine
(Solarbio, G0200) at 37°C with 5% CO₂. HEK293T cells (ATCC, SNL-015) were cultured in DMEM
(Invitrogen, 31053036) supplemented with 10% FBS (Ausbian, VS500T) at 37°C with 5% CO₂. Both
cell lines were authenticated by STR profiling by the supplier and were routinely tested to ensure they
were free of mycoplasma contamination.

Plasmid
The full-length human VDAC1 coding sequence was amplified from human cDNA and cloned into the
pcDNA3.1(+) vector to construct the pcDNA3.1-VDAC1 plasmid. All newly generated plasmids are
available from the corresponding author upon request.

USP30 inhibitor
The MF094 inhibitor (MCE, HY-112438) was dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) to create a stock
solution of 125 mg/mL. Prior to administration, the stock solution was diluted 10-fold with corn oil
(Abmole, M9109). Daily intraperitoneal injections of the diluted solution were administered to mice at
a dose of 30 mg/kg.

Fluorescence-based USP30 enzyme activity assay
Recombinant human USP30 (rhUSP30; R&D Systems, #E-582) was diluted to 25 nM in assay buffer
(50 mM Tris pH 7.5, 100 mM NaCl, 0.1 mg/mL BSA, 0.05% Tween-20, 1 mM DTT) and 5 µL was
added to each well of black, clear-bottom 384-well plates (PE, #6008280). Two point five µL of MF094
was added in each well. After 30 min pre-incubation at room temperature, 2.5 µL of Ub-Rho110
substrate (R&D Systems, #U-555; final 50 nM) was added to initiate the reaction (final volume: 10 µL).
The plate was incubated for 1-2 hours at room temperature, with inhibitor-only and enzyme-only
controls included. Fluorescence was measured at 485 nm excitation and 540 nm emission.

Cell-based apoptosis assessment
Cells from AT2 organoids were digested using Dispase II and TrypLETM as above mentioned and
seeded for apoptosis assay at a density of 50,000 cells per well in a 96-well plate which has been pre-
coated with a 1:20 diluted Matrigel for 2 hours. MLE12 cells were seeded at 20,000 cells/well in a 96-
well plate and pretreated with MF094 for 2 hours. HEK293T cells were seeded at 20,000 cells/well in
a 96-well plate and transfected with 200 ng pcDNA3.1-VDAC1 plasmid using Lipofectamine 2000
(Invitrogen, 11668) 24 hours before the following assay.

For apoptosis detection, the cells were treated with 1 mg/mL bleomycin (Vokai Biotechnology, 9041-
93-4), incubated with IncuCyte® Caspase-3/7 Green (Sartorius, 4440) at 1:1000 dilution and
monitored by IncuCyte® live cell system in real time. The ratio of cells undergoing apoptosis was
calculated as the number of green fluorescent cells divided by the total cell areas.

Bone marrow derived macrophage (BMDM) culture
Both WT and Usp30-/- BMDMs were isolated and cultured as follows: mouse femurs and tibias were
ground and the bone marrow was flushed with sterile PBS, filtered through a 40 µm cell strainer and
centrifuged. The cell pellet was resuspended in RPMI-1640 medium (Invitrogen, C11875500CP)
supplemented with 10% FBS (Ausbian, VS500T), 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Thermo, 15140122), and
1% HEPES (Invitrogen, 15630080), plated at 8 million cells per 10 cm non-treated dish and incubated
at 37°C in a 5% CO₂ atmosphere. On day 4, 5 mL of fresh medium was added. On day 7, cells were
digested with 2 mM EDTA for 10 minutes at 4°C. The macrophages were collected and plated at
800,000 cells per well in a 12-well plate. For polarization, cells were stimulated with LPS (100 ng/mL;
InvivoGen, tlrl-eklps) and IFN-γ (20 ng/mL; R&D, 485-MI-100) for M1 polarization, or IL-4 (20 ng/mL;
PeproTech, 214-14) for M2 polarization. After 24 hours, cells were collected for RNA extraction and
qPCR analysis.

Lung fibroblast culture
Both WT and Usp30-/- fibroblasts were isolated from mouse lungs by flow sort based on EpCAM-CD31-
CD45-, as detailed in the flow cytometry section. The flow-sorted fibroblasts were cultured in DMEM
(Invitrogen, 31053036) supplemented with 10% FBS (Ausbian, VS500T) and 1%
penicillin/streptomycin (Thermo, 15140122) and used between passages 2 and 5. For fibroblast
activation assays, WT and Usp30-/- fibroblasts were seeded in a 12-well plate at the density of 50,000
per well for RNA extraction, or in 8-well chamber slides at a density of 200,000 cells per well for
immunofluorescence. Cells were stimulated with 4 ng/mL of TGF-β1 (R&D, 240-B-010) for 48 hours,
followed by RNA extraction for qRT-PCR or fixation and staining. To evaluate fibroblast proliferation,
WT and Usp30-/- fibroblasts were seeded in a 96-well plate or in 8-well chamber slides at the density
of 20,000 per well and cultured with or without 10% FBS (Invitrogen, 31053036) for 48 hours followed
by CellTiter-Glo assay (Promega, G7571) or EdU analysis. For EdU analysis, 10 µM EdU was added
4 hours prior to harvest, followed by staining as described in the EdU incorporation section. For
apoptosis assessment, fibroblasts were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 20,000 cells per well.
The following day, cells were changed to serum-free medium and cultured for 48 hours followed by
caspase-3/7 activity determination using IncuCyte® Caspase-3/7 Green (Sartorius, 4440) as
described in the cell-based apoptosis assessment section.

Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM)
Freshly collected lung samples were fixed in 2.5% glutaraldehyde in PBS at room temperature for 2
hours, followed by PBS wash and post-fixation in 1% osmium tetroxide in PBS for 1 hour. After that,
the samples were dehydrated through a graded series of ethanol (30%, 50%, 70%, 90%, and 100%)
and embedded in epoxy resin. Ultrathin sections (70 nm) were cut using a Leica Ultracut UCT
microtome and collected on copper grids. The sections were then stained with 2% uranyl acetate for
15 minutes and lead citrate for 5 minutes to enhance contrast. SEM imaging was performed using a
GeminiSEM460 Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscope, with a minimum of 20 cells per sample
examined to ensure representative imaging.

To quantify mitochondrial morphological parameters and perform 3D reconstruction, SEM images
were analyzed using a customized computational pipeline. Mitochondrial segmentation was performed
using Cellpose v4106 with a CPSAM model that was pre-trained on mitochondrial datasets and
subsequently fine-tuned through multiple rounds of iterative training (≥10 rounds) using manually
annotated SEM images from our samples until achieving a segmentation accuracy exceeding 90%.
The resulting binary masks were analyzed in ImageJ (Fiji) using the Analyze Particles function to
quantify mitochondrial counts and cross-sectional areas. For 3D reconstruction, serial ultrathin
sections (70 nm thickness, n ≥ 100 consecutive sections per sample) were first aligned and registered
in TrakEM2 (Fiji) to correct for cutting-induced distortions, followed by mitochondrial segmentation
using the optimized Cellpose model. Aligned segmentation masks were subsequently imported into
Amira software (v6.0, Thermo Fisher Scientific), where the following steps were performed
sequentially: interactive thresholding, surface generation, surface smoothing, and surface visualization.
This workflow enabled precise assessment of mitochondrial morphology and spatial structure.

Tissue preparation and immunofluorescence (IF)
The freshly dissected mouse left lungs were inflated with 600 μL fixation solution (4% PFA, 50% OCT)
and fixed at room temperature for 1 hour, followed by PBS wash, overnight dehydration in 15%
sucrose and 50% OCT and subsequently OCT embedding. The tissue block was sectioned into 6 μm
slices using a Cryostat Microtome (ThermoFisher Scientific). The sections were fixed with 4% PFA for
5 minutes, treated with 0.1% sodium borohydride (Sigma Aldrich, 213462) in PBS for 10 minutes,
blocked for 1 hour in blocking buffer (PBS supplemented with 1% BSA, 5% horse serum and 0.1%
Triton X-100), and incubated with the primary antibody at 4°C overnight. The next day, the sections
were stained with a fluorescent secondary antibody for 1 hour at room temperature, followed by DAPI
staining for 15 minutes, and then mounted for imaging.

For Tyramide Signal Amplification (TSA) staining, the tissue sections were processed using a TSA kit
(ABclonal, RK50026P) with modifications to the standard immunofluorescence protocol described
above. Following sodium borohydride treatment, endogenous peroxidase activity was quenched by
incubation with Peroxidase Blocking Buffer for 15 minutes at room temperature in the dark. After three
washes with PBS, blocking and primary antibody incubation were performed as previously described.
The sections were then incubated with HRP-conjugated rabbit polymer secondary antibody (1:1000)
for 1 hour at room temperature. Immunofluorescence signals were developed by incubation with the
fluorescent tyramide working solution for 10 minutes at room temperature. Nuclei were counterstained
with DAPI for 15 minutes, and the sections were mounted for imaging.

The antibodies used in this study included rabbit anti-pro-SPC (1:3000; Millipore, AB3786), goat anti-
pro-SPC (1:1000; Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-7706), mouse anti-pro-SPC (1:50; servicebio,
GB154201), rat anti-RAGE (1:400; R&D, MAB1179-100), rabbit anti-phospho-Histone H3(Ser10)
(1:500; Sigma-Aldrich, 06-570), rabbit anti-LC3B (1:100; Sigma Aldrich, L7543), mouse anti-ACTA2-
conjugated FITC (1:200; Sigma Aldrich, F3777), rabbit anti-ACTA2 (1:500; Abcam, ab5694), rat anti-
KRT8 (1:100; DSHB, MABT329M) and rabbit anti-USP30 (1:50; ThermoFisher Scientific, PA5106762).

Quantification of immunofluorescence
For quantification of immunofluorescence staining of tissue sections, the entire lung lobes were
imaged using the Nikon Ti2-E CSUC-W1 Sora camera system (Nikon, Japan), except that Cy7 signals
identifying mitochondrial autophagy in AT2 cells were acquired using the STELLARIS 8 Falcon FLIM
Confocal microscope (Leica Microsystems, Germany). The Trainable Weka Segmentation (TWS)
plugin in Fiji/ImageJ was employed to quantify the areas of ACTA2+, RAGE+, and their corresponding
DAPI+ regions. SPC+ areas were manually outlined in ImageJ by selecting regions with homogeneous
SPC distribution. For quantification of organoid cultures, SPC+, RAGE+, phospho-Histone H3+, and
EdU+ cells were quantified using QuPath v0.5.1 with “Analyze → Cell Detection → Positive Cell
Detection” module. For the quantification of mitophagy, QuPath v0.5.1 software and module were
employed. Each mitochondrion was identified based on the mito-Dendra2 signal. The colocalization
of LC3B with each mitochondrion was used to determine the mitochondrion undergoing mitophagy,
and mitophagy index was calculated as the ratio of LC3B+mito-Dendra2+ to total mito-Dendra2+
mitochondria.

Western blot
Snap-frozen mouse lungs were ground into powder on dry ice and lysed in RIPA buffer supplemented
with Protease Inhibitor Cocktail (Roche, 11697498001), 1mM phenylmethyl sulfonyl fluoride (PMSF)
and Phosphatase Inhibitor Cocktail (Sigma Aldrich, 524625-1SET). Protein concentration was
measured using the Pierce BCA protein assay kit (ThermoFisher Scientific, 23227) and equal amounts
of protein lysates were loaded for SDS-Page. The primary antibodies employed were β-Actin (1:1000;
Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-47778), VDAC1 (1:400; Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-390996),
Cleaved caspase-3 (1:1000; Cell Signaling Technology, 9661S), USP30 (1:500; ThermoFisher
Scientific, PA5106762), COL1A1 (1:1000; Cell Signaling Technology, 72026S), ACTA2 (1:200; Abcam,
ab5694), LC3B (1:500; MBL M152-3), P62 (1:500; Santa Cruz, sc-48402), Phospho-Ser65-Ubiquitin
(1:1000; Cell Signaling Technology, 62802S) and pro-SPC (1:400; Millipore, AB3786). The secondary
antibodies used were goat anti-mouse conjugated HRP (1:5000; Thermo Fisher Scientific, G21040)
and goat anti-rabbit conjugated HRP (1:5000; Thermo Fisher Scientific, G21234).

Measurement of Phospho-Ser65-Ubiquitin levels
MLE12 cells were seeded in 12-well plates at a density of 200,000 cells per well. Cells were pretreated
with MF094 at concentrations of 0, 1, 5, 10, and 20 µM for 2 hours prior to the addition of 10 µM CCCP
for 4 hours. Cells were harvested and the protein lysates were prepared for Western blot analysis.

RNA extraction and qPCR analysis
For RNA extraction, the Eastep™ Super Total RNA Extraction Kit (Promega, LS1040) was used for
tissue samples, while the HiPure Total RNA Nano Kit (Magen, R4125) was employed for cell samples.
Complementary DNA (cDNA) was synthesized using a reverse transcription kit (Vazyme, R222-01).
Subsequent qPCR analysis was conducted with SYBR qPCR Master Mix (Vazyme, Q711-03).
Relative gene expression levels were determined using the ΔΔCT method and normalized to HPRT.
The primers utilized in this study are listed in Supplementary Table 1.

RNA-seq analysis
AT2 cells (CD45- EPCAM+ CD31- Integrin β4-) were flow-sorted from the lungs of influenza-infected
mice at 0, 2, 6, and 11 days post-infection. Sftpc-traced AT2 cells (tdTomato+) were flow-sorted from
tamoxifen-treated WTΔSftpc and Usp30ΔSftpc mice at day 14 after saline or bleomycin administration, or
at day 14 after influenza infection. Following RNA extraction, library preparation was performed using
the TruSeq RNA sample preparation kit (Illumina, RS-122-2102) according to the manufacturer's
protocol. Sequencing was conducted on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform, generating 150 bp
paired-end reads. Raw sequencing data were processed using bcl2fastq (Illumina) to convert base
call files to FASTQ format. Quality control was performed using FastQC (V0.12.1) to assess the
FASTQ files.107 Reads were aligned to the Mouse Genome Assembly GRCm38 using HISAT2
(V2.2.1).108 The resulting alignment files were processed to generate gene expression counts using
featureCounts (V1.22.2).109 For the time-course samples, differential expression analysis was
conducted using edgeR (V3.40.2).110 For Sftpc-traced AT2 cell datasets (saline, bleomycin, and
influenza groups), differential expression analysis was performed using DESeq2 (V1.38.3).111 Gene
set enrichment analysis (GSEA)112 and KEGG pathway analysis were performed using
clusterProfiler113 (V4.1.2). For saline-treated Sftpc-traced AT2 cells, the log fold changes of
mitochondrial genes were compared to those of background genes (non-mitochondrial genes).
Cumulative distribution function (CDF) curves were generated using the ggplot2 package (V3.4.4) in
R, and the statistical significance of the distribution shift was assessed using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov
(KS) test.

For re-analysis of published microarray data (GSE110147),41 raw CEL files were processed using the
R packages affy114 (V1.76.0) and limma115 (V3.54.0), with differentially expressed genes defined as
|log FC| ≥ 1 and p value ≤ 0.05. GSEA and correlation analyses were performed using
clusterProfiler113 (V4.1.2) and cor.test function, respectively.

Single cell RNA-seq analysis
CD45+ and CD45- cells were flow-sorted from bleomycin treated WT and USP30-/- mice (n= 4 mice /
group) and processed using the Chromium Single Cell Platform (10X Genomics, Pleasanton, CA).
Libraries were prepared according to the manufacturer's protocol and sequenced on an Illumina
NovaSeq 6000 system. The CD45+ and CD45- library yielded 79,493 cells with an average sequencing
depth of 22,802 reads per cell. Raw sequencing data were processed using Cell Ranger v8.0.1 (10X
Genomics) for initial quality control. Subsequent analyses were performed using the Seurat
package116 (v4.3.0) in R. We applied stringent quality filters, excluding cells with fewer than 200
detected genes or >25% mitochondrial gene content. After quality control, 78,379 high-quality cells
were retained for downstream analysis.

Data normalization and feature selection were performed using SCTransform. Dimensionality
reduction was achieved through principal component analysis (PCA), with the top 20 principal
components serving as input for UMAP visualization. Cell clustering was performed using the
FindClusters function (resolution = 0.8), and cell type annotation was based on canonical marker gene
expression patterns. To evaluate specific cellular phenotypes and metabolic states, pathway activity
scores were computed using the AddModuleScore function in Seurat with default parameters. For
fibroblasts, functional states were assessed using gene sets for proliferation (Mki67, Pcna, Top2a,
Ccna2, Cdk1, Ccnb1), apoptosis (Bax, Casp3, Casp8, Fas, Bid, Bcl2l11), and differentiation (Acta2,
Col1a1, Fn1, Postn, Cthrc1, Spp1). For AT2 cells, metabolic profiles were characterized using gene
sets for glycolysis (Pkm, Ldha, Gapdh, Hk2, Eno1, Pgk1, Pfkp), mitochondrial stress (Hspd1, Hspa9,
Clpp, Lonp1, Yme1l1), nuclear-encoded OXPHOS (Ndufa9, Ndufb8, Sdhb, Uqcrc2, Atp5a1, Cox5a,
Cox4i1), and mitochondria-encoded OXPHOS (mt-Nd1, mt-Nd2, mt-Co1, mt-Co2, mt-Atp6, mt-Cytb).

The published scRNA-seq data of IPF lungs (GSE135893)42 was reanalyzed using the Seurat116
(V4.3.0) package in R (V4.2.2). Differential gene expression analysis between IPF and control samples
was performed using the FindMarkers function with default parameters, followed by gene set
enrichment analysis (GSEA)112 to identify significantly altered pathways.To assess mitophagy and
oxidative phosphorylation activity scores, we retrieved the corresponding gene sets from the Gene
Ontology database (GO:0000423 for mitophagy and GO:0006119 for oxidative phosphorylation).
Cellular pathway activity scores were calculated using Seurat’s AddModuleScore function116 (V4.3.0)
with default parameters, enabling quantitative comparison across cell populations.

Human sample collection
Human lung tissues were obtained from Tongji University Affiliated Shanghai Pulmonary Hospital.
Specifically, normal lung tissues were obtained from macroscopically normal tissues adjacent to
pulmonary nodules during surgical resection, and IPF lung tissues were obtained from the explanted
lungs of IPF patients undergoing lung transplantation. Participants were not compensated. To protect
participant anonymity, exact ages have been replaced with age ranges in our data presentation.
Following the SAGER guidelines, participant sex (3 females and 7 males) was determined based on
self-reported medical records. Due to the limited sample size used exclusively for immunoblotting,
sex-based analysis was not performed. All human tissue samples were completely destroyed during
the protein extraction process for immunoblotting analysis, and no samples were conserved for further
analysis. Detailed de-identified characteristics of the human tissues are listed in Supplementary Table
2.

Statistics and Reproducibility
Custom scripts in R v4.2.2 were utilized for RNA-seq and scRNA-seq data analysis and plotting. All
other statistical calculations were analyzed using GraphPad Prism version 9.0 (GraphPad Software,
San Diego, CA). Statistical tests used and the sample size is indicated in corresponding figure legends.
The exact p-values are shown in figures or figure legends. A p value of <0.05 was considered
statistically significant. All data are generated from three or more independent experiments with at
least three biological replicates per genotype and condition. Investigators were blinded to group
allocation during the quantitative assessment of imaging analysis and lung function monitoring. For
biochemical assays and computational sequencing analysis, blinding was not applicable as group
identity is required for downstream comparative pipelines. No statistical methods were used to
predetermine sample sizes. Sample sizes were empirically chosen based on established standards in
pulmonary research, which provide sufficient statistical power to detect biological differences in injury
models.

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript identifies USP30 as a novel therapeutic target in lung injury. The authors employ both global and AT2-specific genetic knockout models, providing compelling evidence that USP30 inhibition promotes lung regeneration in diverse injury contexts, including bleomycin-induced fibrosis and influenza-induced pneumonia. Mechanistically, USP30 depletion reduces AT2 cell apoptosis via VDAC1 following injury while enhancing their proliferative capacity, thereby limiting alveolar damage and promoting regeneration. Overall, the study provides important insights into USP30 as a regulator of alveolar repair and highlights mitochondrial dysfunction as a promising therapeutic avenue, but several points require clarification and further analysis.
Major Points:
1. Clarify whether USP30 deletion affects mesenchymal/fibroblast populations (apoptosis, proliferation, or differentiation) and whether fibroblasts show transcriptional changes in scRNA-seq.
2. Assess whether mitochondrial functions beyond mitophagy (e.g., oxidative phosphorylation) are altered in scRNA-seq data.
3. Determine if USP30 is expressed in transient cell states (DAPT/PATS/K8+) and whether knockout in AT2 cells impacts these populations post-injury.
4. Evaluate potential effects of USP30 deletion on distal bronchiolar stem/progenitor cells (secretory cells, BASCs, LNEPs).
5. Provide clarification on the design of the floxed allele and possible reasons for limited recombination efficiency in AT2-specific KO mice (Figure S3B). Could this be related to the sequence length between two loxP sites in the floxed USP30 allele, making excision less efficient even with the robust Sftpc-CreERT2 driver?
6. Include lineage-tracing data (tdTomato) in AT2-specific KO experiments (Figure3) to better distinguish AT2-derived regeneration from bronchiolar stem cell contributions. More precise quantification of AT2 proliferation (tdT+ vs tdT–) is needed.
Minor Points:
1. The statement that USP30 KO “does not affect” fibroblasts or macrophages may be too strong according to limited data here; consider rephrasing.

### Reviewer 2

Wu et al. investigate the role of USP30-mediated mitophagy in promoting alveolar regeneration following lung injury. The authors used genetic and pharmacological approaches targeting Usp30 to demonstrate that loss of USP30 enhances mitophagy and restores mitochondrial function in AT2 cells, thereby protecting them from apoptosis and promoting regenerative capacity. The findings are interesting and provide a fresh insight into the cellular mechanisms of tissue repairing. The study nicely shows that Usp30 deletion reduces AT2 apoptosis and promotes proliferation across multiple lung injury models. It can be further strengthened to examine the link between USP30 loss and changes in the AT2 cell transcriptomic profile with or without injury, providing evidence how USP30 loss enhances AT2 stem cell activity at the molecular level. A few other minor issues are listed below.
1. The authors performed scRNA-seq for Usp30-/- and control mice followed by bleomycin challenge. It is interesting that no pathological fibroblasts were identified. This reviewer wonder if the authors examine pathological fibroblasts markers Cthrc1 and Postn?
2. Figures S1I and S1J: Saline-treated controls can be further analyzed. Data on mitochondrial number and function in uninjured lungs would strengthen the baseline comparison.
3. Figures 3A–3C: It is unclear whether observed mitochondrial morphology and gene expression changes are specifically from AT2 cells. Additional validation such as AT2-specific isolation or imaging would clarify this point.
4. Figure 3C heatmap and KEGG analysis: The comparison focuses on time points rather than genotypes. It would be more informative to directly compare WT and Usp30⁻/⁻ gene expression profiles to identify pathways altered by USP30 loss.
5. The authors cultured AT2 organoids in AMM-based medium as described in Ref 91. It seems that AT1 cell differentiation rarely happens if cultured in AMM. It is interesting that the authors detected quite a number of AT1 cells in this culture system (Fig. 2L, M). Did the authors modify the medium?

### Reviewer 3

Studies by Wu et al, analyzes the susceptibility to lung injury and fibrosis by inhibition of USP30 using genetic and pharmacological approaches. Studies analyze the bleomycin induced lung fibrosis and the influenza pneumonia murine models. Studies show that inhibition of USP30 in AT2 cells is sufficient to increase resilience against lung injury. Investigators hypothesize inhibition of USP30 promotes AT2 proliferation by an ROS mediated mechanisms and protection against apoptosis by reducing VDAC protein levels. The studies are relevant to the field and have translational potential. However, there are some concerns that need to be addressed.
1. The significance of the studies, especially the translational potential, will be enhanced with evidence of higher expression of USP30 in AT2 cells of human lung fibrotic diseases like IPF. Similarly, if changes in ubiquitination and protein levels of VDAC1observed in the current mouse studies are relevant for the human fibrotic disease.
2. scRNAseq data do not align with the other set of data of the manuscript. For example, the proportion of myofibroblasts that the authors show increase by IFA are not shown, nor the cluster of fibrotic fibroblasts CTHRC1+ that produce high levels of ECM. These changes will confirm the effect in fibrosis by the absence of USP30. Similarly, it would be important to define the cluster of proliferating AT2 to confirm the EdU and organoid experiments. Additionally, there is lack of AT1 cell cluster. The AT2-AT1 cluster shown in the UMAP data has a limited proportion in comparison with the abundant Ager+ staining shown in Figure 2.
3. Interestingly, studies in Figure 2 and 2S show that AT2 cells of WT mice in naïve conditions have active apoptosis in contrast to AT2 from USP30 KO. Authors suggest that this apoptosis is related to high levels of VDAC protein. It is unclear what is the stimuli for overexpression of VDAC1 in naïve healthy AT2 cells to mediate apoptosis. Furthermore, transcriptomic data is needed to demonstrate that changes in VDAC in USP30 deficient AT2 cells are not associated with transcriptional changes and only are related to changes in ubiquitination and protein degradation.
4. The high levels of mtROS in AT2 from USP30 KO mouse are in contrast to the increase in maximal respiration shown in the seahorse studies for KO cells. High maximal OCR generally is associated with a state of low mtROS generation and mitochondrial fitness. Furthermore, it is unclear why there are not changes in the mitochondrial TMRM and mitochondrial mass between mouse strains if mitophagy is induced differently between groups. Simultaneous analysis of these two parameters might help to give a better understanding as well as complementary markers of autophagy like p62 protein levels, and ubiquitination of Parkin to analyze mitophagy. Furthermore, studies of mitophagy flux in the AT2 cells might be also useful.
5. Figure 1M do not show markers of cell type to define if AT2 cells have been analyzed for the colocalization of mitochondria and LC3B. it seems that USP30 deficiency increase levels of LC3B.
6. The authors in line 162 suggest enhanced mitochondrial biosynthesis in AT2 from USP30 KO suggested by mitochondrial morphology and number. Complementary studies of markers of mitochondrial biogenesis and dynamics are recommended to support the statement.
7. Figure 4B shows inhibition rate of the Compound MF094, however it will be more specific to show the effect of the compound on the ubiquitination of a known mitochondrial protein target of USP30.
Minor concerns
1. The measurements for OH-Pro for bleomycin and influenza pneumonia lung models have more data points than other experimental variables, suggesting than more than 1 sample per lung mouse was analyzed. There is not a description in this respect on methods. Please clarify.
2. The USP30 protein expression and levels after deletion were not analyzed
